Recent breakthroughs in text-to-speech systems have revealed the limitations of existing methods. To overcome these limitations, we introduce MaskedSpeech, a novel framework that generates more expressive and natural speech with fewer resources. Building on the foundations of existing TTS systems, we propose an innovative approach that masks key frames from the acoustic targets to create a more unrestrained search space for our unsupervised speech synthesizers. By maximizing the correlation between the masked frames and the simulated targets, as well as maintaining the original frame sequence, the MaskedSpeech training objective strikes a balance between optimizing acoustic parameters and preserving the original temporal structure. As a result, our method demonstrates substantial improvements in naturalness and expressiveness over existing baseline techniques in unsupervised TTS.

The focus of variable selection within Bayesian linear regression can be those variables whose probability distributions are confident in their contributions to predicting the outcome. While retaining posterior uncertainties for unselected variables, we propose a novel framework that utilizes a hierarchical model with an additional layer of uncertainty to enforce sparsity. This enforced sparsity affects the concentration parameters of the normal-gamma prior distributions on the model coefficients, allowing retention of posterior uncertainties for unselected variables through its separation from the shrinkage process. Furthermore, we introduce the notion of reference kits for selecting a limited number of relevant variables from a vast number of variables. Through simulations and real-world data applications, we demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed approach over benchmark techniques.

Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to attacks that can deceive their outputs. Typically, these attacks involve manipulating test data to alter classifications. This research investigates Man-in-the-Middle attacks on DNN classifications, which involve modifying both the input data and the communication process between the DNN and its input. Unlike conventional attacks, which focus on the data-only channel, this study explores the potential of exploiting the entire communication process. Moreover, four novel attacks are introduced, which can be conducted without modifying the DNN training process. To protect against these attacks, several defense techniques are presented, including a method to detect manipulation detection, an authentication system for both data and communications, and a verification process to confirm the integrity of both the data and its source. An evaluation of these attacks and defenses demonstrates their effectiveness in preventing manipulation of the data, communications, and subsequent classifications.

Our analysis focuses on the spread of climate change conspiracy theories in social media groups. Our initial findings reveal that a single group accounts for the majority of content sharing on platforms such as Twitter and Reddit. Through content analysis, we uncover the prevailing narratives among members who engage with this content. Furthermore, our investigation shows that this group utilizes a specific set of words and phrases to maintain consistency in their conspiracy theories. Finally, our examination of member profiles confirms that the group's consensus holds significant influence within the group.

The initial findings from the LUX153 experiment's dark matter data have been thoroughly examined using cutting-edge analytical tools. These results reveal no significant difference between the observed data and predicted values from various theoretical models, with a level of agreement that is consistent with other dark matter experiments. To further validate the analysis, a comprehensive evaluation of systematic uncertainties was conducted, with the outcome confirming the reliability of the results. Additionally, the capability of detecting rare events in the LUX153 experiment's data has been utilized to set a limit on the cross-section of dark matter nucleon interaction, with the result in line with existing constraints from other experiments.

Building upon the framework of exangulated categories by Kontz, Nakaoka and Palu, we explore Serre duality within this context, focusing on projective objects in relation to the existence of Serre duality. A necessary and sufficient condition for Serre duality to apply is that the category has a projective object whose codelection set is representable. This condition also necessitates that the category has enough projectives. Furthermore, under this condition, we establish the dualisation of morphism sets in exangulated categories. In addition, we discuss first results applying this concept to triangulated categories and Krull-Schmidt exangulated categories.

This study measures and compares the returns on investment to different post-secondary fields of study in three countries: Norway, Denmark, and Sweden. The analysis uses a 20- to 30-year follow-up period and controls for individual characteristics, family background, and field of study. The results show significant earnings disparities across fields of study in all three countries, with significant variations in the magnitude and pattern of these disparities. The findings also reveal substantial variations in the pattern and magnitude of these disparities both within and outside of vocational education. When comparing the three countries, significant differences emerge in the magnitude and pattern of these disparities, with significant variations in the returns on investment to different fields of study in Norway and Denmark contrasting with Sweden. The reasons behind these discrepancies lie in the different structures of education in each country, with significant variations in the nature and funding of vocational education in Norway and Denmark.

A new generation of experiments is eagerly anticipated at the BESIII detector at the BEPCII collider, dubbed a'super $J/ho$ factory', due to its exceptionally high production rate of the $J/ho$ meson. This research facility will offer an ideal setting for an in-depth analysis of the $J/ho$ and other charm particles, notably the $E^0$ states. The proposed program of research is comprehensive and will encompass a range of topics, such as the spin and parity characteristics of various hadrons, the assessment of quark pair creation assumptions in photon-photon interactions, the search for anomalous heavy flavor hadron decays influenced by extra dimensions, the study of rare or electroweak transitions in the $T$ and $E^0$ region, and the $J/ho$ hadron production mechanism across different energy scales. The projected studies will significantly contribute to advancing the understanding of particle physics, further refining theoretical models, and opening up new avenues for theoretical investigation.

Our study investigates how a binary star system affects the accretor in a hierarchical three-body configuration. The more massive binary in our experiments either orbits centrally or has a slightly eccentric path. The accretor is comparable to a single star of the same mass, with its accretion behavior distinct from a purely binary system. As the less massive body in the binary passes closer to the accretor, it experiences enhanced emission due to strong gravitational interaction, eventually being ejected in most cases. The accretor's mass increases by up to a tenfold in successful mergers, with its growth influenced by the orbital energy of the passing body. The outcome of our experiments supports the notion that a binary system increases a massive star's cross-section for mergers by at least an order of magnitude, with a larger binary having a greater effect. This effect is consistent across various mass ratios of the binary system components.

Using the theoretical framework of Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker models, our study examines how inhomogeneous distributions of matter affect the universe's structure from the Big Bang to the present. We investigate the impact of these distributions on the universe's gravitational field, which influences the motion of particles and galaxies. Employing the post-Newtonian method to analyze gravitational effects, our findings show that inhomogeneities influence the universe's gravitational field, leading to deviations from the predicted motion based on a uniform energy density. We also analyze the stability of galaxy clusters, considering the impact of inhomogeneities, and our results support the concept of stable galaxy clusters. We then calculate the scale factor of the universe's curvature, using observed data and the motion of galaxies within galaxy clusters.

We first analyze the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model under general assumptions and derive a necessary condition for its minimizers. This condition enables us to introduce a new objective function, which is a modification of the original by incorporating the total variation of the gradients within each segment. This modified function aligns with the proposed non-convex optimization problem, whose local minimizers it closely resembles, especially in the case of piecewise-homogeneous images. We also present an algorithm to solve this optimization problem and evaluate the adapted model through both theoretical and experimental validation. The results show that this new approach yields better segmentations for images with corrupted pixels.

The capabilities of atomic interferences were used to investigate whether ultra-light particles of a specific type exist in a state of quantum degeneracy. Our analysis has revealed that if this type of particle exists in such a state, it is highly unlikely to constitute the majority of dark matter found in the universe, due to constraints imposed by the temperature and entropy levels left behind by the particle. Our research considers the possibilities of particles with mass smaller than the electromagnetic scale, ruling out the likelihood of such particles accounting for the bulk of dark matter unless they are very rarely created. Conversely, particles with masses above the Hubble scale at early times can efficiently form the basis of dark matter, but would need to be given an initial boost in energy density relative to normal matter.

In neuromorphic computing, on-chip learning allows analog hardware to adjust its parameters according to sensory data stream. This process doesn't involve complete numerical representations, overcoming significant challenges associated with analog learning. On-chip learning can utilize spike-based training, either through spike-dependent plasticity or digital synapses, and often relies on the same hardware used for offline training. This process can take place either within a single device or multiple devices communicating with each other. This study focuses on spike-dependent plasticity and explores its potential to develop robust features suitable for classification tasks. Our classification results show promising performance, particularly in tasks where temporal patterns play a crucial role, and we observe feature structures similar to those obtained through spike-and-trap learning methods. However, the features extracted through spike-dependent plasticity undergo significant changes when the training data is modified, highlighting the need for spike-dependent feature extraction. Conversely, spike-and-trap learning-based features exhibit increased stability in response to altered training data. Additionally, our results show that digital synaptic encoders can efficiently decode spike sequences even in the presence of noise, and that on-chip learning can develop robust features capable of providing accurate class labels even when the training data and test data differ significantly.

A comprehensive examination of 20 MHz frequency band noise storms at Jodrell Bank has yielded significant insights into intense noise creation and its dynamic behavior. By analyzing the spectral evolution, researchers discovered that intense noise storms exhibit a characteristic growth pattern akin to a sausage mode, with their intensity directly correlated to their size. This finding suggests that intense noise storms are likely generated by a single plasma source, and their growth is facilitated by a parallel magnetic field. Furthermore, the observation of a cooling effect in some noise storms suggests that a technique called two-temperature model could effectively model their frequency spectra.

A dual-layer magnetophotonic trap is designed using finite-difference time-domain simulations to optimize a magnetooptical trap's efficiency. This innovative design integrates the magnetooptical trap in a planar structure, facilitating compact integration with microchip technology. By aligning the trap's layers at a 45-degree angle, the efficiency of the design is enhanced. Compared to a conventional setup, this integration enhances capture efficiency and minimizes the trap's size, achieving a nearly seven-fold reduction. The improved efficiency and geometric compactness make this design suitable for scalable and efficient photon collection from cold atoms.

The powerful radio jets emitted from certain supermassive black holes (such as those in M87 and Cygnus A) seem to be in a state of high energy output, despite the relatively low energy emitted from their central black holes. It has been suggested that the high energy of these jets could be the result of the black hole powering an accretion disk that is partially obscured and thus reducing the measured energy output of the black hole. If this is the case, it is likely that a similar process occurs in the less powerful black holes at the centers of our galaxy (Sgr A*) and the Milky Way (indicating that these less powerful black holes may still generate and produce energy in the form of high-speed particles emitted from the accretion disk).

The work examines a scenario in which a neutral atom travels past a planar mirror, focusing on a specific instance where the atom is initially aligned with the mirror and then moves at right angles to it. The study considers a brief, pulsed light emission from the atom in the absence of any external influence, followed by the investigation of how the mirror impacts the emitted light. The research reveals that the mirror's effect transforms into a scattering of the emitted light, resulting in distinct observation possibilities. The study provides a detailed analysis of the photon scattering probability in terms of the atom's initial and final positions. Additionally, the findings show that the photon scattering probability exhibits periodic fluctuations, peaking at around 40% when the atom is at its farthest point from the mirror.

A longstanding mystery surrounds the origin of the cosmic rays powering the interstellar electron acceleration that led to the formation of pulsar wind nebulae and the diffuse gamma-ray background. Another theory suggests that supernovae from young massive clusters might be a key source, thus we examined the electron production rate in the Westerlund 2 cluster to test this hypothesis. A combination of multiwavelength observations and Monte Carlo simulations revealed a supernova rate of approximately one every 30,000 years, with a significant fraction of these being massive stars that could give birth to compact objects capable of generating pulsar wind nebulae. However, this rate showed considerable variation based on different assumptions, suggesting that a different explanation for the gamma-ray background is likely needed.

The minimax principle is a renowned tool that leverages the properties of a functional to derive existence properties in variational problems. Despite being extensively applied in physics and engineering, it remains a relatively understudied topic in mathematics. In our research, we expand on this principle by deriving a new version specifically tailored for orientation-dependent functionals. This revised minimax principle is then applied to prove the existence of minimal solutions for a critical problem in harmonic maps that involves homotopy constraints and orientation-dependent functionals.

Degraded document images can be enhanced and made clearer through the assistance of super-resolution networks. However, these improvements can also lead to errors in text recognition if sub-optimally achieved. This paper proposes enhancing text recognizers with a Generative Adversarial Network component, allowing them to critique and judge recognized text in context. To efficiently train and optimize this hand-written text recognizer, it is combined with a hand-written synthesizer. This fusion integrates the capabilities of a hand-written text synthesizer to simulate and simulate recognition errors, thereby supplying the recognizer with realistic, generated counterfeits to judge during training. This hybrid model was tested on the H-DIBCO challenges and outperformed other competing systems by surpassing all evaluation metrics.

The widespread adoption of ID cards offers opportunities for easily gathering a considerable amount of text data. This paper examines the use of Machine Learning and Natural Language Processing to develop an automated system for extracting ID card text, which could also include a built-in lie detection feature via a Fraud Detection System. Our proposed system leverages Deep Learning and NLP to analyze the extracted text and identify potential fraudulent activities. Our method has demonstrated exceptional accuracy in extracting ID card text and accurately classifying transactions as legitimate or fraudulent in the Reuters Challenge dataset.

This research focuses on LTE and 5G channel estimation under rapid movement conditions. Leveraging large memory capabilities of LSTM neural networks, a proposed LSTM-based channel estimator aims to account for channel variations generated by user equipment in motion. By utilizing this model, initialized with relevant parameters, channel estimator operates in a standalone manner without needing channel estimation data. Our simulation-based study validates the substantial performance enhancements achieved through LSTM-based channel estimation, particularly in scenarios involving high levels of mobility, outperforming a conventional method employing traditional LSTM for channel representation.

We utilize a Bayesian algorithm centered on the Hyper-Laplacian Prior (HLRIP) to create sharp images from blurry ones. Astronomical observers often encounter problems of distinguishing between noisy images due to limited telescopes and real signals from objects. As a result, the process of extracting information from these images is significantly hindered. To address this issue, our method is able to enhance fuzzy images and detect the underlying structures within them. To test its effectiveness, we applied the algorithm on a set of simulated images and the actual observations of a specific planet, and compared its accuracy to other existing methods. Additionally, our code has been made available for other researchers to use.

We've developed an innovative neural network algorithm designed to automatically create expressions for element-wise multilinear operations. Examples of such operations include Hadamard product and entry-wise multiplication. The proposed algorithm generates a neural network, known as a multilinear operator network (MOP), for each input variable or function on a specific domain. The neural network is trained to replicate the behavior of the multilinear operation in question, utilizing only the operation's stochastically sampled inputs and corresponding outputs. To prevent overfitting, a regularisation technique is employed, where a weight for each MOP is initially set to zero, and only updated during training if the difference between the operation's actual output and the MOP's prediction exceeds a specified threshold. This regularisation process is done in batches for efficiency. As a result, only the MOP weights for the particular input variable or function being trained on are updated. The method has been successfully tested on a variety of multilinear operations and shown to be highly effective.

In 2021, the ECFA formed an Early Career Researchers' panel to represent its young professionals and address specific issues at the association and national levels. This panel began official activities in January and has been working to define its scope, objectives, and approach since then. In this report, the panel outlines its initial outcomes and planned areas of focus for future development.

The unique properties of graphene enable us to study its theoretical limits in the optical domain, allowing for the analysis of graphene-based structures at their theoretical maximum - where all possible states are utilized. By doing so, we identify an unsupervised protocol for generating line waves via spatially confined terahertz radiation. Our findings indicate that utilizing the full potential of graphene's electronic properties enhances the energy carried by these waves, as their conductivity approaches the theoretical maximum of the Drude model. Through this approach, we develop scalable graphene patches that produce line waves with high energy levels and narrow spectral overlap, as well as wider spectral overlap at lower energy levels. This technique can be applied to multiple graphene nanoscale technologies to amplify the energy carried by these waves, reducing the necessary graphene size to achieve a desired effect.

The joint training of multiple robots and multiple human partners through Federated Learning is a novel approach to collaborative learning. This training method enables independent entities to collaborate on a shared task by exchanging and integrating local models. We've developed a new FL framework that accommodates the unique requirements of multiple, autonomous entities. This framework facilitates the efficient training of systems comprising multiple robots and multiple human partners by automating the process of model exchange and update. Furthermore, our framework provides adaptive communication protocols to minimize data transmission and power consumption. Through comprehensive simulations, we've validated the effectiveness of our approach and demonstrated its significant power consumption savings compared to conventional FL methods.

This research introduces a new nonparametric estimator that weakly converges to the true parameter under a specific condition, maintaining its bias-reduced structure.  A key contribution of this work is the development of an innovative bias-correction technique, yielding an efficient and computationally feasible method that accommodates a broader class of conditions than current bias-reduced estimators.  Furthermore, this paper expands on previous research by demonstrating the consistency of a specific type of bias-corrected estimator, a finding that has significant implications for the consistency of certain estimators in statistical models.  To illustrate the effectiveness of this new approach, we include simulation studies demonstrating its performance in practical applications.

Knowledge graph link prediction is a significant task in knowledge graph completion that focuses on identifying unseen triplications. Many KLP methods rely on relation extraction to enhance triplication generation, but few consider the influence of extraction errors. We introduce RELEAS, a framework that simulates extraction errors in knowledge graph completion by generating triplications from existing PGs with artificial errors. The framework supports various error types and can be applied to different KLP methods. By examining the effects of errors on KLP performance, we analyze the robustness of six prominent KLP methods and provide guidance on how to minimize the impact of errors in future relation extraction tasks.

In 2020, Ghosh et al. discovered the Debye mass for charged Yang-Mills theory had multiple solutions, each corresponding to specific charge types. We have extended their work, introducing various chemical potentials for different charge types while maintaining thermal equilibrium. Our analysis shows that introducing a muon chemical potential reverses the order of certain Debye mass solutions, while making another solution vanish. Similarly, introducing a muon chemical potential for baryons also alters the order of certain Debye mass solutions and sets two previous solutions to zero. Our findings align with expectations from holographic QCD, providing further evidence of its semi-quantitative accuracy.

Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 exhibit antiferromagnetic properties. 
The magnetic arrangements in these materials feature alternative patterns of magnetic poles within sublattices labeled Ru1 and Ru2, with the latter exhibiting a different configuration compared to Tb3RuO7.
The origin of these magnetic structures has been attributed to competitive self-assembly tendencies between Ru1 and Ru2 ions, with the latter being more susceptible to magnetic ordering. 
The applied pressure may modulate the magnetic arrangements in these materials, with the effect being more pronounced in Nd3RuO7.

Our research introduces an novel representation of functions using a specialized neural network, optimized using a functional approximation technique, to enhance generalization capabilities. This new representation excels at capturing signal characteristics in limited-dimensional scenarios. We provide empirical evidence of its benefits and show that it can be approximated by standard neural networks within a defined functional space. Additionally, our experiments highlight the representation's effectiveness in real-world scenarios, such as image and video classification, and we make our code and datasets publicly available.

In various contexts, researchers have attempted to separate a dependent variable from an independent variable using models, although a general method is yet to be established. Most existing models are based on specific assumptions regarding the variable relationships. In contrast, we introduce a new model framework that distinguishes causes from effects by learning bidirectional relationships between variables, without relying on prior knowledge. The proposed semi-generative model can be applied across different scenarios, including synthetic and real-world data sets. To enforce the directionality of relationships, we utilize a novel variant of graphical models, allowing for the interpretation of model results. Furthermore, to enhance the model's capacity to handle complex data sets, we have developed an optimization algorithm for parameter estimation. Experimental evaluations have demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed model in accurately determining the directionality of relationships for both simple and complex data sets.

This paper explores the unexplored area of applying topological methods in deep learning through a comprehensive literary review. We delve into the topological structure of deep learning systems, analyzing their design and functionality from multiple perspectives. Furthermore, we investigate deep learning's potential applications to topological problems. Ultimately, the study examines the reciprocal influence of deep learning and topological computing, which is a burgeoning field known for its analytical and computational tools.

Consider a cubic field of discriminant $d$ and let $\sigma(\omega_d)$ denote the principal part of its embedding map. We introduce the concept of "lattice minima" and investigate their properties in relation to fields of degree 3. It is demonstrated that for specific radicands, the lattice minima fail to satisfy a central criterion, whereas the outcome is favorable for fields with discriminants exceeding the discriminant of the field defined by $\sqrt{3}+\omega_d$. The proof involves showing compliance with a specific conjecture proposed by Chen, then using that result to prove an extended form of an existing inequality originally derived by Saroch and Strzecha.

Deep neural networks' (DNNs) immense success in data interpretation is paired with the difficulty of understanding their internal workings. Despite breakthroughs from other fields, interpreting DNNs remains an unresolved issue. This research presents a novel framework that enables a deeper understanding of how DNNs learn and make decisions. By extending an existing explanation method, our framework allows it to be applied across various DNN architectures. We also develop a new, adaptive explanation metric that effectively captures both individual and group interpretation capabilities. This understanding eventually enables the construction of interpretive modules within DNNs, which can be used to train them from an interpretative perspective. We thoroughly evaluate our framework across multiple DNN architectures and uncover that the insights gained facilitate data visualization, enhance generalization capabilities, and make the DNN more robust to adversarial attacks. Ultimately, the insights gained enable the creation of deeper neural networks that are more robust and reliable.

The \r-associated Stirling numbers of the second kind, denoted as,\rS(n,k), are a generalization of Stirling numbers of the second kind. In the special case where r equals 1, the \r-associated Stirling numbers reduce to standard Stirling numbers of the second kind. For small values of n and k, along with r, an explicit formula for \rS(n,k) is given. Furthermore, a lower bound for \rS(n,k) is provided, utilizing the convexity of the logarithmic function. Additionally, an explicit formula for the normalized sum of \rS(n,k) when n equals 10 is given. In the context of weakly increasing sequences, \rS(n,k) represents the number of such sequences with exactly k elements, facilitating the determination of sequences with a sum of r that does not exceed n.

The deposition of a second material layer on a first one constitutes the most fundamental change that can occur in a three-dimensional bulk building block, known as a layered material. To gain insights into the chemical and physical properties of these layered materials, we have developed a comprehensive system to classify their possible configurations. By maximizing the size of the active area in which electrons can move and interact, we have identified the top candidates for this classification. These candidates are broken down into distinct categories, each with its own set of basic building blocks. These building blocks are then applied to a list of over 1000 materials to predict a wide range of layered materials. Many of these materials are found to have properties similar to those of transition metal oxides and dichalcogenides. By studying the electronic properties of these materials in both theoretical and real-world contexts, we have confirmed that they can be used to create a wide range of devices that can carry currents in one direction but not the other, among other properties.

We examine the relationship between the maximum achievable momentum and the size of a space-time region, given that its volume or surface area has a minimum size dictated by the de-Broglie wavelength. This leads us to investigate whether the total number of possible momentum states is limited, and we show that in scenarios involving curved space-time, a maximum momentum is indeed imposed. In order to explore this, we develop an alternative form of the Klein-Gordon equation for massive particles moving on a Schwarzschild manifold, and use it to derive an approximate relationship between momentum and radius that applies to both massive and massless particles.

We introduce an innovative method to efficiently use complex-valued affine coupling layers in Monte Carlo simulations by leveraging unitary matrices in its construction. This approach involves parameterizing affine coupling layers using complex values and exploring its relationship with the complex affine transformation of Gaussian distributions through the Jacobian determinant. We develop a search method for optimal complex parameters that minimizes the Monte Carlo error, making the method suitable for realistic simulations. Furthermore, we investigate the potential of our method and demonstrate its effectiveness in sampling from complicated multivariate distributions.

We present a realistic model featuring the minimal U(1)_F flavor symmetry breaking to differentiate the quark masses within a specific charge. This is achieved by having two flavons with similar U(1)_F charge, resulting in a non-trivial arrangement that breaks the symmetry. Furthermore, we show that our model can naturally produce significant mass hierarchies between quarks, such as the large gap between the top and bottom quarks, as well as the small PMNS phase, θ_e, within the Standard Model.

This research explores the risks associated with the malicious deployment of private keys extracted from Virtual Private Networks, specifically Keyless Virtual Private Networks, which are not secured with a passcode. By conducting a thorough examination of the KVPNs' source code, scientists were able to identify the patterns in the unencrypted, random keys generated by each VPN service and their corresponding cyclic patterns. By using this knowledge, hackers can steal the private keys by analyzing the encryption keys, a process the researchers call Virtual Privilege Chain Management. The team was able to successfully demonstrate the practical application of VPPMs in three distinct environments, using randomly generated keys, which enabled them to bypass security measures and gain unauthorized access to systems. Furthermore, the team discovered that, in many cases, the encryption keys can be directly mapped to the VPPM fingerprints. By using these mapped key-fingerprints, hackers can create custom VPPMs to gain privileged access to systems, which underscores the significance of protecting the VPPMs with robust passwords.

The widespread adoption of pre-trained language models has created both a challenge and an opportunity for developing models tailored to lesser-resourced languages. In this study, we examine the extent to which pre-trained language models can be adapted to languages without significant data availability, measuring adaptability through tasks involving no prior knowledge of the target language and limited, high-cost data availability. By comparing zero-shot and few-shot adaptations of Monolingual Language Interface (MLI) and Multilingual Language Interface (MLI) models to Russian using resources in English, German, and French, we identify that: (1) both methods exhibit comparable adaptability; (2) using an existing multilingual model offers a more efficient path to adaptation than building a monolingual model from scratch; and (3) having pre-trained models in a related language (German in this case) significantly accelerates adaptation. Our findings support the use of multilingual models for adapting to resource-constrained languages, and highlight the potential of zero-shot and few-shot adaptations to expand the range of tasks and languages that can be efficiently processed.

Within a rotating core, matter begins to collapse in a specific direction. Initially, its shape resembles a symmetrical, mass-concentration core. As it collapses further, a binary system emerges at its center, with properties influenced by its angular momentum. By examining various models of cores with different angular momentum, a pattern emerges: in cores where angular momentum leads to significant equatorial plane mass concentrations, the binary mass grows in relation to the kinetic energy invested in its formation, compared to those with more even mass distributions. This discovery could offer a new explanation for the observed correlation between binary masses and their energy investment and may provide insights into how binary systems develop under various conditions.

The construction of the m-ar-K (m-uple-arcsine-Kohonen) function is rooted in probability distributions, specifically utilizing the arcsine distribution based on multipoles. This concept evolves from the conventional ar-K (arcsine-Kohonen) function, which employs radial hyperplanes. The proposed m-ar-K function enhances dimensionality reduction techniques, particularly for datasets with high dimensions and a small number of samples. Unlike traditional methods, m-ar-K operates effectively in scenarios where the number of features surpasses the number of samples. Additionally, m-ar-K can be applied to handle data sets containing negative values, addressing a limitation of its predecessor, ar-K, which is restricted to non-negative values.

A proposed model called Extended Polynomial Calculus for Boolean Circuit Satisfaction (EPC) has connections with other probabilistic models. It's suggested that EPC contains a stronger version of Polynomial Time (PTIME). If a super-polynomial EPC lower bound is established, it could imply that PTIME is essentially equivalent to Deterministic Time t^n for some large 't'. This could have significant implications for the relationship between Classically Parallel Time (CPT) and PTIME. A CPT-PTIME collision would mean that CPT is essentially non-differentiating in relation to PTIME operations. A super-polynomial EPC lower bound could also influence our understanding of the relationship between CPT and PTIME, potentially allowing us to construct CPT-PTIME collisions. Furthermore, it's proposed that EPC contains CPT, and that PTIME contains a weaker version of EPC compared to NP. If a super-polynomial EPC lower bound is achieved, it could enable the construction of EPC-PTIME collisions. Building on this, it's suggested that EPC contains a stronger version of CPT compared to PTIME, allowing for the construction of EPC-PTIME collisions. All these relationships are model-specific and not necessarily transferable to other probabilistic models.

A noetherian ring with $\sigma$-derivation satisfies ideal unity if all its ideals are $\sigma$-invariant and generate the ring when combined. We establish that if a ring with derivation $\sigma$ is $\tau$-nil-derived (meaning $\tau(\sigma(x)y=0$ implies $xy=0$)) and has non-zero derivation $\sigma$, then it is $\sigma$-elementary and satisfies ideal unity. Furthermore, if a ring has non-zero derivation $\sigma$ and $\tau$-nil-derived, then the conditions of being $\sigma$-elementary and satisfying ideal unity are equivalent.

The sheer scale of social media narratives makes comprehensive human-driven analysis impossible, forcing us to rely on semi-supervised or unsupervised methods. Despite their efficacy, these methods often fall short due to the inherent limitations of their output, hindering their potential to guide informed policy decisions. To address this gap, we introduce NarrativeExplorer, an innovative framework that uses Topic Modeling and Network Analysis to extract actionable insights from large social media datasets. By leveraging Twitter's 1.6 million posts related to gun control, we demonstrate NarrativeExplorer's capability to identify recurring themes, interconnected ideas, and key stakeholders, thereby providing policymakers with a deeper understanding of public sentiment and informed outcomes.

This paper introduces an event detection system capable of processing spatio-temporal data across diverse spatial resolutions. The framework relies on a hierarchical structure of convolutional neural networks, where each node represents a location within a city, and employs attention mechanisms to pinpoint event onset sites. A novel loss function is proposed to address uneven data distributions. The framework effectively handles events occurring across varying spatial resolutions and can detect their temporal correlations. The system also learns to recognize locations based on their spatial resolution. The framework's performance in addressing the partial observation problem and adaptable resolution issues will be demonstrated using benchmark data from New York City. Furthermore, the approach's ability to identify event resolution will be exhibited using data from Chicago.

We've made the first direct measurement of how galaxies behave due to gravity's effect on light bending in the cosmos. The result will help reduce uncertainties in plans to use galaxy clustering as a precision tool for understanding the universe. The measurement was based on a specific method using the microwave background radiation's effect on light to map gravitational fields, and was made with the help of data from the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope's predecessor program. The measurement took into account the uncertainty associated with a specific type of noise in the data, and found that its impact had a minimal effect on the result. The result will likely be confirmed by future data from the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope and the Euclid space mission.

We introduce a novel framework that provides robustness to significant data corruptions for deep learning models through worst-case perturbation theory. This framework involves solving a convex optimization problem to obtain a robust model, yet it has limitations in real-world applications due to its practical unfeasibility. To address this challenge, we propose an iterative algorithm based on semidefinite programming that yields a viable solution. However, this solution remains optimistically robust as it relies on an accurate estimation of the worst-case perturbation. To counteract data corruption, we develop a data preprocessing technique that utilizes our theoretical framework, effectively utilizing the robust model to preprocess data. This technique, known as the worst-case robust adjustment, can be computed efficiently and enhances the robustness of existing models through iterative refinement. We evaluate the proposed framework in theoretical calculations and experimental tests, demonstrating its success in providing robustness to significant data corruptions for various models and datasets.

To create a realistic model for the spread of rumors, we examine the process of information diffusion in an online environment. The model utilizes a system where the peak and attenuation coefficients are influenced by the characteristics of initial information and physical location. Applying the forward Kolmogorov equation allows us to analyze the temporal and spatial evolution of the rumor spread. Our numerical simulations reveal the importance of initial information, spatial location, and their interactions in controlling the spread of rumors. Additionally, we propose a simple optimization method to determine the optimal forward speed of the rumor.

An in-depth examination of feature reduction techniques for hyperspectral data is conducted, emphasizing the comparative analysis of different dimensionality reduction methods. Twenty-eight prominent dimensionality reduction techniques are critically evaluated based on their performance in hyperspectral pixel classification. To ensure uniformity in comparison, a comprehensive framework is developed using 20 well-known datasets. Notably, methods like LLE, ISOMAP, LAD, and NNC are found to yield high signal reconstruction capabilities while achieving effective classification outcomes. The investigation also explores the impact of intra-class and inter-class distances, dataset density, and noise levels on the performance of these dimensionality reduction techniques. Furthermore, a correlation study is performed to identify the relationships between reconstructed energy and accuracy scores of different methods. The findings of this study provide insights into the performance of conventional dimensionality reduction techniques in hyperspectral pixel classification, enabling researchers to select the most suitable techniques for their applications. To facilitate easy comparison, the method performance metrics are visualized using bar charts, tables, and scatter plots, ensuring that the results are easily accessible to researchers.

Deep neural networks are known for their exceptional performance in various application domains, but they pose significant challenges due to their substantial size, rendering them difficult to deploy in resource-constrained environments. Consequently, researchers have been actively seeking efficient ways to compact these complex networks. In this paper, we provide an in-depth analysis of various network compression techniques, including pruning, quantization, compact architecture design, and compression of pre-trained models through knowledge distillation. We also introduce a new strategy called group sparsity, offer an innovative method for compressing arbitrary networks, and experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of existing and proposed compression methods on different image classification benchmarks, achieving an exceptional balance between accuracy and efficiency.

Protein structure refinement using expert knowledge often results in enhanced predictions.
ProCS: A highly accurate expert-guided approach to protein structure refinement, leverages expertise from multiple sources of protein contact statistics to accurately predict high-precision protein structures.
ProCS utilizes a network of expertise by incorporating accurate statistical information regarding residue-residue distance and angle in protein structures.
ProCS effectively mitigates challenges posed by noisy and distorted data through the application of expert guidelines.
Furthermore, the method demonstrates superior performance in refining proteins containing multiple domains.
ProCS surpasses other structure refinement methods in predicting high-precision protein structures.
ProCS is now available for public use at the website of the University of California, Los Angeles.

Optimizing machine learning models often relies on selecting the right loss function, yet sometimes widely used loss functions can lead to subpar performance, despite being simplified or regularized. This study investigates under-represented loss functions and assesses their potential in improving model performance. It specifically evaluates KL Divergence on a variety of classification tasks and discovers that incorporating prior knowledge through regularization can enhance model accuracy. Furthermore, the research explores data augmentation techniques to expand the training dataset, demonstrating that using Divergence includes essential information previously missing from other loss functions. As a result, models trained with KL Divergence exhibit improved generalization performance on classification tasks.

We develop the parquet theorem for quantum spin systems with the fewest possible interactions that apply to all relevant dimensions. By representing the Hamiltonian in a sum of ladder and Yang-Baxter operator forms, we express the model's amplitude using these components, leading to two different expressions: one derived from Hamiltonian-based analysis and another through conventional parquet methods. Although the two models agree under the condition $ab=0$, their properties otherwise differ significantly in terms of conservation and crossing symmetry. Furthermore, the Hamiltonian-based model exhibits conservations analogous to those seen in thermodynamic Bethe ansatz equations, whereas the conventional model lacks this property. This theoretical construction provides an alternative to standard parquet methods for calculating two-particle correlations in interacting spin systems. We apply this framework to a specific Heisenberg model to compare its two-particle correlations with those of a related mean-field model over a range of parameters.

Starting with a review of the general theory of exciton condensation, we delve deeper into the emergent superfluid properties observed in monolayer TiSe2. Through a Hubbard-like tight-binding model incorporating both vertical and lateral intercell Coulomb interactions, we demonstrate that an exciton condensate can be achieved by transforming a charge-density-wave state derived from the initial Mott insulator into a superconducting-like state at finite lattice commensuration. Under the condition of equal Coulomb intercell interactions in all directions, the exciton condensate is shown to spontaneously adopt a 2D current of charge at an exact commensuration wave vector. Additionally, we examine how this exciton condensate is impacted by an external electric field that introduces dissipation and drives the system towards a normal state characterized by thermal mean-free path or quasi-normal coherence length.

To identify incidents' nature and scope more quickly, many organizations with dispersed workforces use an automatic dispatch service that receives text-based reports from users. These incident reports vary depending on the situation, but often contain irrelevant information that slows down dispatchers. To address this issue, a researcher examined 185,000 incident records from a real-world system to categorize the content and identify common elements in each category. The analysis revealed that while variable in content, incident reports typically include information about users' locations, health, and property. To streamline the incident response process, a researcher suggested creating separate channels for certain types of incidents and proposed two models to help automatically detect the scope and scale of incidents based on report text. The models achieved high accuracy rates of 0.942 and 0.985, respectively, when tested on a large dataset. The researcher plans to investigate whether incorporating additional data, such as users' locations and histories, can further enhance the incident response process.

In a number of materials with unusual topological characteristics, like Weyl semimetals and Dirac semimetals, the overall structure of the Fermi surface plays a crucial role in determining their magnetic properties when they transition into superconducting phases. The overall shape of the Fermi surface exerts a significant influence on the superconducting state's response to an external magnetic field. The overall structure of the Fermi surface exerts a significant influence on the superconductive critical field and its behavior in external magnetic fields. Active learning algorithms seek to efficiently select a limited number of unlabeled samples for optimal training. Traditional methods often rely on the accuracy of labeled data or approximate predictions from a well-trained classifier, but these assumptions are not always met in practice. This paper critiques the conventional approach of using model uncertainty as a guide for sample selection and proposes a semi-supervised minimax entropy-based method. This novel technique ensures diversity in chosen samples by maximizing the mutual information between the initial and updated pools of labeled data. Additionally, it restricts the chosen samples to be as difficult as possible to classify. To overcome the computational challenges associated with optimizing this non-differentiable objective function, a provable alternative based on the entropy approximation of a non-differentiable function is developed. Experiments conducted on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed technique over existing active learning algorithms.

The researchers conducted an extensive analysis of song audio from the Internet to examine the concept of timbre over time. Utilizing the magnetic alignment technique to create playlists based on audio similarity, the investigators discovered that the songs on the playlist are similar in timbre. Furthermore, the study ranked songs by popularity and found that the playlists followed a chronological pattern, with similar audio characteristics appearing in songs from the same decade. Interestingly, the most well-known songs in each era formed their own distinct groups in terms of timbre, resembling separate categories.

This work focuses on analyzing the behavioral patterns of a stochastic process that incurs rewards, using block analysis. We investigate both the expected number of blocks and their diversity, by considering the maximum number of unique blocks up to a given time. Our findings reveal that, as time progresses, both of these values asymptotically converge to infinite. We also demonstrate that, under certain conditions, the distribution of the maximum number of blocks, observed at a specified time, converges towards a log-normal distribution.

The initial objective of Proof-Net Theorem is to establish a correspondence between the semantics of cut-elimination in sequent calculus and the semantics of nested sequences of reasoning based on containment relationships. To achieve this, we introduce the concept of nested sequences of reasoning as nested proof-nets and explore how the process of cut-elimination corresponds to the optimization of these sequences through contraction. Furthermore, we examine how the procedure of taking the converse of a nested principle translates to the concept of reversal, revealing that this operation does not alter the converse relationship among the resulting principles. As a result, we can conclude that the converse relationship among the nested principles of a proof-net is optimal, which in turn allows us to provide a sequential reorganization of the proof-net that reflects this optimal relationship. Additionally, we propose an interpretation of the cut-elimination theorem within the framework of nested domains, which involves showing the equivalence between the nested domains resulting from the application of the reverse contraction operation and the domains generated by cut-elimination in sequent calculus.

Using human feedback efficiently is a critical aspect of reward learning. Rather than process individual experiences one by one, leveraging comparisons from multiple experiences at once can significantly make the most of human feedback. Nonetheless, the central challenge lies in ensuring the comparisons provided by humans cover all relevant aspects. Current batch reinforcement learning algorithms struggle to scale due to their reliance on either pre-defined comparison functions or extensive exploration to guarantee completeness. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach that eliminates the need to pre-define comparison functions or carry out extensive exploration. Our proposed algorithm, ComparaRL, generates critical feedback comparisons through its analysis of experience correlations. As a result, ComparaRL is capable of learning comparison functions efficiently, ultimately leading to improved performance on complex benchmark tasks without relying on pre-defined functions or extra computational resources for comparison generation. Moreover, ComparaRL scales significantly better than state-of-the-art batch reinforcement learning methods, as evidenced by our experimental results.

The Smyth powerspace is defined as the topological space $\Sigma^\Delta X$ where $\Sigma^\Delta X$ represents the Smyth powerspace of $X$, and the open subspace topology on $\Sigma^\Delta X$ is derived from open subsets of $X$ being mapped to open sets in the Löbspace $\Sigma^\dag X$. Powerspaces initially emerged in the context of domain theory; however, the variant employed by Smyth has distinct topological characteristics and the construction preserves core-compactness in general. Yet, it is known that the Löbspace topology on an arbitrary domain does not need to be core-compact. Researchers have recently demonstrated that the Smyth powerspace topology is the smallest core-compact topology that can be applied to $\Sigma^\Delta X$, and this paper provides an alternative proof of this fact by establishing a direct relationship between the Smyth powerspace topology and the topological properties defined by Johnstone's "topological valuations", specifically showing that the Smyth powerspace is core-compact because it satisfies the T0 valuation property.

The paper introduces a configuration space called pointed vortex loops, which is topologically equivalent to a two-dimensional plane with a puncture. It demonstrates that for a fixed area, the configuration space of vortex loops with a fixed number of points has the topological characteristics of a two-dimensional sphere. Additionally, the study shows that the universal cover of this configuration space is similar in structure to the ordinary cover of a plane with a puncture, and a specific family of curves, known as pseudoholomorphic curves, is used to establish this result.

A fundamental challenge in causal inference lies in efficiently estimating the counterfactual mean in high-dimensional settings. The AIPW method offers an efficient solution that involves combining estimators for the counterfateful means. Yet, a critical issue arises when dealing with model irregularities, where the standard AIPW estimator becomes biased and inefficient. This paper addresses the problem in settings with treatment selection based on multiple factors. By introducing L1 regularization, the AIPW estimator can be made unbiased and efficient, although highly efficient. This paper develops an alternative AIPW estimator that uses a linear combination of the befit estimators, where each is derived from a different form of regularization. The proposed estimator is shown to be asymptotically efficient and unbiased under certain conditions. The efficiency of this estimator is confirmed through simulation results and an empirical analysis conducted in the context of the High School Core Curriculum study.

The tau lepton's substantial mass renders it susceptible to various physical influences such as form factors, momentum processes, and loop corrections. To investigate this phenomenon, researchers use lattice Monte Carlo simulations to construct an interaction matrix incorporating the tau's spin and momentum. In doing so, they can determine the tau's electromagnetic and hadronic form factors by comparing the resulting matrix with experimental data. Additionally, the technique allows for assessing the tau's decay into light particles, a process influenced by a specific type of correction. The researchers tested this approach with data from the HMC algorithm and investigated the form factors' accuracy in relation to different lattice spacings.

Researchers investigated the behavior of baroclinic waves within a rotating, fluid annulus with a horizontal axis, using both experimental and analytical methods. By initiating the system from a state of equilibrium and observing the development of the Baroclinic Wave Instability, they were able to gain insights into its structure and dynamics. High-resolution measurements of the flow within the annulus allowed them to detect the presence of the Baroclinic Wave Instability through surface deformations and predict the characteristics of the dominant eigenfunction associated with it. Notably, the shapes of the eigenfunctions matched those obtained from theoretical predictions, with the amplitude of the fluctuations increasing proportionally to the square root of the distance from the center of the system. This investigation provides a framework for the approach to stability analysis in this particular system.

We explore a Bayesian approach to estimate extreme value models, starting with a polynomial model for simplified understanding. The tuning parameter'm' is a crucial aspect that leverages prior knowledge to focus on most likely patterns, and its selection impacts model fit and forecasting. A flexible'm-sensitivity' analysis is conducted to evaluate how changes in'm' influence model performance and identify a suitable range. Following the basic model, more complex Bayesian representations for extreme value models are developed and applied to real-world data, taking into account prior knowledge of a site's flood behavior. Using Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations, model parameters are estimated and a likelihood-based comparison highlights the superiority of the proposed models. Finally, predictive distributions are obtained for future flood events, and a popular measure of forecast accuracy is applied.

Incorporating principles from economics to model agent behavior realistically results in reinforcement learning problems being susceptible to data corruption. A common assumption in existing studies is that the extent of corruption can be known, enabling the development of robust algorithms. This paper, however, investigates the scenario where the amount of corruption is unknown and must be estimated. We have found that determining the amount of corruption is a non-trivial problem, and it is not possible to create algorithms that can robustly handle large-scale corruption while also providing optimal performance in clean data without additional resources. In the context of parameter-free algorithms, we propose a new sample selection method that can robustly handle corruption on a limited scale and provides comparable performance to existing methods under clean data. Additionally, we have designed a new data storage system, which can efficiently handle corruption and provides optimal performance under clean data without relying on prior knowledge. Both algorithms show promising results in practice, exceeding the performance of existing methods in scenarios where the amount of corruption is limited.

The impulsive heat equation is a modified impulsive second order equation that models heat propagation within a bounded domain with exterior influences. This paper investigates the approximate controllability of this equation using finite dimensional controls, under conditions on the spatial variable. The impulsive heat equation has been studied previously, but controllability was only established for a specific finite dimensional control space. This paper expands upon that work, providing a framework that determines the controllability of a wider range of controls without restrictions on spatial variable assumptions. The approach utilizes feedback controls and an approximation operator to show finite dimensional approximate controllability. Furthermore, an operator for approximating controls is developed and the impact of its spectrum on controllability is explored.

Detecting when models go off the rails in the real world remains eluded.
Past research on out-of-distribution detection has mostly been conducted using
synthetic data generated from known distributions, but such methods fall
short when confronted with out-of-distribution data drawn from shifting
prior distributions, changing class conditional distributions, and mixed
class labels. Our investigation aims to expose these limitations and hold
models to account. A new set of detection data, dubbed 'Challenge Data',
has been created by combining data from established datasets and altering
it in various ways to simulate real-world anomalies. Our findings
demonstrate that contemporary methods are unable to effectively detect
anomalies in the Challenge Data. In response, we introduce a novel method,
called Hybrid Density Estimation, that utilizes the strengths of both
density estimation and classification to detect anomalies. Our results
demonstrate that this new method substantially outperforms the alternative
methods when tested on the Challenge Data.

In the study of molecular motors, past research highlighted the influence of stochastic forces, such as molecular interactions and temperature-driven fluctuations, but neglected the impact of electric currents. Although motor proteins are insensitive to electrical energies in biological contexts, this phenomenon becomes relevant at the cellular level when motor proteins are subjected to currents from scanning tunnels or electrochemical reactions. As molecular mechanics continue to evolve, incorporating these non-biological forces may provide valuable insights. This research extends the existing models of motor dynamics to account for the effects of electric currents. Utilizing a mathematical model of electrostatic interactions, our analysis demonstrates that current-induced forces can significantly alter the dynamics of motor movement. This is illustrated by examining an idealized system of motor molecules experiencing a Brownian motion in a simulated force field. The outcome reveals that the direction of the motor's motion is determined by the direction of the electric current and the charge of the motor, while its speed is controlled by factors such as its charge, size, and properties of the scanning surface.

A one-way and non-deterministic two-way word transducer is being analyzed to ensure it has an equivalent version with only one way and a regular resynchronizer that is also bounded and equivalent to a given one-way transducer. It has been proven that if a specific two-way transducer and its equivalent one-way transducer both map a given word to a specific word, then there also exists an equivalent one-way transducer that is similar to the original two-way transducer but maps to the given word. Additionally, it has been proven that any non-deterministic two-way transducer can be replaced with a one-way and bounded transducer that is equivalent in a specific way, and also that if a certain one-way transducer and its equivalent two-way transducer both map a given word to a specific word, then there also exists an origin-equivalent two-way transducer that is similar to the original one-way transducer but maps to the given word.

Our analysis reveals that calculating a specific entry in the f-Convolvation can be done in $O(mn\log n\log m)$ time, which is more efficient than computing the full convoluation. Furthermore, a fast entry computation algorithm for the f-Kerouvation is achieved in $O(mn)$ time. To validate our results, we prove a lower limit of $\Omega(mn)$ for the time complexity of entry computation in the f-Kerouvation. 

In the realm of programming languages, dynamic memory allocation is often optimized using pools to reduce random access times. For numerical computations, splitting pools into distinct segments based on access frequencies allows for efficient organization. A high-frequency segment can contain recently accessed elements, while less frequently accessed elements can be shifted to lower segments. 

A program can dynamically acquire memory blocks of the same size from a segment corresponding to the current access frequency. When a memory block is deallocated, it is retained in the associated segment. 

Aimlessly scattering memory blocks across all segments may lead to decreased overall performance, even though each segment contains frequently accessed elements. Therefore, a mechanism to track memory locations and efficiently move deallocated blocks to less frequently accessed segments is necessary. 

As a consequence of this optimization approach, the time required to determine the next available location within a segment of a specific frequency can be significantly faster than a random memory address lookup.
