By analyzing their mental processes, the goal is to identify areas for enhancing the system to improve content management and discover new features to enable researchers. Building upon earlier work, this study expands the scope of examination and introduces a novel model for tag switching that identifies groups of related tags. Additionally, it explores how content creators organize information using these tags and how their tagging strategies relate to their expertise areas. To demonstrate the system's capabilities, it is applied to the datasets of two research areas: research sentences and full documents.

Recent breakthroughs in acoustic metamaterials have led to groundbreaking possibilities in contemporary physics research and technology applications. However, the influence of thermoviscous effects in these materials is often overlooked, especially at microscopic scales where viscothermal limitations can be substantial. To address this gap, we experimentally investigate the thermoviscous behavior of a type of acoustic metamaterial called "knight-of-the-realm" structures, examining the phenomenon through a combination of experimental and numerical analyses. Notably, the introduction of thermoviscous effects yields significant accuracy improvements when modeling this type of metamaterial, underscoring the importance of considering these effects in designing high-frequency acoustic metamaterials.

This paper explores the long-time behavior of the FENE dumbbell model subject to a low-frequency condition. Specifically, the model's solutions are shown to reside in a weakly stable equilibrium state within certain Besov spaces, with decay rates established and a gain of regularity demonstrated. Furthermore, the model's solutions are proven to converge strongly to a steady-state in a specific Lebesgue space, and the rate of this convergence is determined. Notably, the effect of the low-frequency condition on the model's behavior is fully captured through the application of classical PDE techniques and the formulation of an appropriate dissipative estimate in a specific Besov space.

A mobile integrated access and backhaul (mIAB) network sets up a mobile hub that shares the same physical space with user equipment (UEs) and provides high-speed backhaul connectivity to the core of the network. This setup promotes group communications by pinning specific UEs to act as mobile hubs for other users within their vicinity. To optimize mIAB-powered group communications, we develop a quality of service (QoS)-conscious placement strategy that maximizes the coverage area of mobile hubs while ensuring sufficient quality of service for users within their range. By modeling the geometry of user groups and their connections to the core, we use a mixed-integer problem to place mIAB nodes effectively. The resulting algorithm provides solutions near optimal performance in simulations within nanoseconds, yielding significant improvements in coverage area and QoS for users over baseline scenarios.

The instability of hyperparameters in algorithm performance has long been recognized, but the complex interactions between them remain poorly understood. By training neural networks on the CIFAR10 dataset using random search, this study reveals that hyperparameters exhibit contractive behavior when paired with their optimal values, but also shows that this interaction is not representative of the entire stable region. Through analytical optimizations and a new revelatory technique called 'Optimal Path Analysis', the researchers uncovered the underlying cause of this contractive behavior, demonstrating that it is not a characteristic of the stable region as a whole, but rather a result of the nonlinear transformation applied to hyperparameters in deep learning algorithms.

The quantization error of electromagnetic field energy, as predicted by Planck and later supported by Einstein and Compton, can be calculated using $h\nu_{ji}$, which corresponds to the energy differences between adjacent energy levels of hydrogen atoms as observed in the Balmer series.

Traditional reinforcement learning benchmark tests use a fixed environment and flat reward system, but in real-world scenarios, policies must adapt to changing conditions and varying rewards sources. To address this limitation, we have developed the Curated Curriculum Curriculum (3C), a new test platform that evaluates the ability of reinforcement learning algorithms to adjust to different and increasingly difficult tasks. 3C incorporates an adaptive learning plan for each agent, tailoring task difficulty to an algorithm's capabilities, promoting efficient training time. We have applied this new test platform to examine the performance of cutting-edge RL algorithms, uncovering discrepancies in how these algorithms handle changing task demands and revealing insights on how to design more resilient agents.

The multi-mirror, multi-lens, cryogenic wide-field X-ray telescope Liger is being developed under a strategic partnership between the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and the European Space Agency (ESA). Liger's design is a hybrid of the Chandra and XMM-Newton telescopes, offering high-resolution images over its 10 times larger field of view compared to either individual telescope. Its cryogenic optics are combined with a room temperature optical focusing system and the Data Reduction System (DRS), responsible for processing the large X-ray images in real-time, will be a key component of Liger. 

Although XMM-Newton has been successfully operating for 20 years, Liger's images, due to its larger field of view, will contain significantly more pixels and data, presenting a challenge for DRS. This implementation of DRS on Liger will utilize a network of processors to segment and distribute the image processing, with a substantial subset of its algorithms already identified, including non-uniformity correction, image filtering, and star finding. 

However, Liger's unique challenge arises from its images being composed of various segments, each observed by a different set of optics, with varying distortions, for which a substantial number of ghosts and image artifacts are anticipated. 

To tackle this complication, a group of researchers conducted an experiment using a prototype of the Liger DRS, implementing a new approach to accurately determine the center of mass of each ghost ring,

The primary goal of this research is to demonstrate the existence of traveling waves in the Couette account of the two-dimensional Euler equations, which are nonstationary and not closely aligned with the Couette flow except at a very specific singular limit. This work is an extension of past research, which had shown the existence of traveling waves but with a strong restriction on their shape. This new finding comes after incorporating a new approach to analyze nonlinear equations. This approach involves revealing a regularity threshold for solutions, above which they can be accurately approximated using small amplitude expansions. Using this approach, we have determined that there is a wide range of possible shapes for traveling waves, and that these shapes depend on a parameter that influences their behavior. This parameter, which determines the strength of a shear flow, can vary from very weak to very strong, thus providing a wide range of possible solutions. This research has significant implications, as it demonstrates that there is a wide range of possible solutions to the Euler equations that are not closely aligned with the Couette flow, even at very small distances from the point of stable equilibrium.

To analyze an optical nonlinear polarizer's ability to control polarization, we utilize a unique combination of Malus' law and Mueller matrix elements. This method not only offers higher sensitivity but also impacts various fields, such as spintronics and nonlinear optics, by allowing for precise manipulation of optical properties. We discuss how this control can be applied to optimize multiple parameters in nonlinear optical processes.

This research investigates specific types of nonlinear equations known as Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equations. By studying a particular initial value problem in one dimension, with a nonlinear equation derived from the KPZ field theory, it has been discovered that the parameter $\lambda$ dictates the existence or absence of solutions. For $\lambda<\lambda_c$, a critical value, solutions to the problem do not exist. In contrast, for $\lambda>\lambda_c$, it has been demonstrated that the solutions derive from small perturbations of an equilibrium state. Furthermore, through the development of an appropriate small-amplitude expansion, it has been shown that for $\lambda>\lambda_c$, solutions to the problem can be represented as a sum of an equilibrium component and higher-order frequency-based components. This analytical method has been successfully applied to two different types of equations derived from KPZ theory: the KPZ equation itself and an equation known as the KPZ-Stochastic Heat Equation (SHE) equation. As a by-product of this research, it has been discovered that the solutions derived from the KPZ equation and SHE equation are closely related to each other in certain critical instances. For example, when $\lambda=\sqrt{2}$, the solutions to the KPZ equation and SHE equation are identical in form.

South Africa's COVID-19 outbreak has resulted in numerous societal and economic difficulties. Initially, there was a significant shortage of publicly available data, which has since been partially addressed. Despite the increasing availability of data, several obstacles persist, including inconsistent data formats and a lack of standardization. This research presents an open-source data integration platform that successfully amalgamated and prepared data from 15 diverse sources across the country. A total of 242 columns from 15 datasets were analyzed to identify inconsistencies and missing data. Following data cleaning, the integrated dataset comprised 242 columns and approximately 4.8 million observations. The outcome demonstrates the effectiveness of our method in addressing data heterogeneity and preparing the data for further research.

We investigate how allowing a limited number of integers in a subset, denoted $A$, influence the occurrence of arithmetic progressions within that subset. Our analysis indicates that if $A$ consists of $k$ or fewer integers and contains elements at a minimum distance of $H$ from one another, then it includes arithmetic progressions of length $N$ and a common difference of at most $k-1$ when $N$ is expressed as the product of two primes, $p$ and $q$, with $q$ being less than or equal to $p^{1/\alpha}$, and further satisfying the condition that the representation of $N$ in base $\alpha$ includes fewer than $k$ digits, plus some additional conditions. This conclusion builds upon an earlier result by Green and Tao, who allowed for the presence of infinite subsets, whereas our work relaxes this restriction to one involving finite subsets with specified spacing between integers. Our result is also expressed in terms of $\alpha$-normal numbers, which were not part of the original work by Green, Tao, and Vu. We expand upon this by demonstrating that if $A$ consists of $k$ or fewer integers and contains an infinite sequence of numbers with an exponent sequence following a specific pattern, then it includes arithmetic progressquences of length $N$ and a common difference of at most $k-1$. This allows us to show that the set containing all numbers of the form $2^{\alpha n+p

The performance of Deep Neural Networks can be enhanced by fusing the predictions of multiple models. Fusion methods are broadly categorized into early, intermediate, and late fusion techniques. Early fusion and intermediate fusion techniques combine features and use them to predict the target, whereas late fusion models make predictions separately and average them. This paper presents a novel approach called Hierarchical Fusion, which starts by training an encoder to integrate information from multiple sources, akin to early fusion. The encoded information is then passed through a decoder to generate class predictions, and class prediction losses are used to refine the representation, mimicking intermediate fusion. This hybrid technique offers superior performance compared to existing fusion methods in the classification of skin lesions. The project's code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishkahlia/HierarchicalFusion.

Hospitals' intensive care units are now overwhelmed with COVID-19 patients who require urgent medical attention and a limited number of available intensive care unit beds. To effectively distribute these critical care resources, there is a pressing need to predict which patients will require intensive care the earliest. A novel, state-of-the-art model has been developed that employs a deep learning technique with a double stacking structure, featuring a 1D convolutional neural network and a transductive learning strategy to estimate the duration until patients need intensive care. Our model's performance in predicting severe COVID-19 outcomes surpasses that of a baseline established by healthcare professionals, yielding a 90.3% improvement in ROC-AUC, 95.6% improvement in F1-score, and 97.6% improvement in order ranking accuracy compared to the baseline. Our model's unique structure and the effectiveness of its features have been thoroughly explained, along with the reliability of its predictions through sensitivity analysis. Based on these results, it is believed that this model has the potential to provide healthcare professionals with early and late warnings about patients who need intensive care during their hospital stay.

This study investigates the number of distinct transmission eigenfunctions that can be found around the boundary of a sphere in a $N$-dimensional space. The research shows that these eigenfunctions are localized within a specific region near the boundary of the sphere by considering the medium's properties. Two constant values representing the medium's properties are presented in the study to illustrate this localization. Consequently, the study's results provide an estimate for the minimum distance between the transmission eigenfunctions' suppression bands around the boundary of the sphere. It's worth noting that this estimate holds only if the medium's properties are uniform, resulting in a simpler scenario for analyzing the transmission eigenfunctions' behavior. In contrast, the medium's properties vary when considering the far field of the transmission eigenfunctions. One exceptional case in which the localization result holds for the variation in the medium's properties is when the dimension of the space is two.

To enhance utterance representation learning using pre-training, we examine how to utilize prior knowledge in transcripts to aid deep utterance models. Firstly, we investigate transcript-informed pre-training objectives such as predicting transcript-based contextual representations or transcript segments. Secondly, we analyze how transcript multi-task learning can be implemented, including utilizing transcript information in pre-training denoising autoencoders. Thirdly, we consider how transcript information can be utilized to regulate pre-training denoising autoencoders and maintain their functionality. Our findings suggest that utilizing transcript information in denoising autoencoders leads to more accurate speech enhancement. Additionally, we discover that utility-driven transcript-informed pre-training can elevate the performance of the downstream speech enhancement task.

The universal bundle functor E: G\^{}{\del} \to G acts as a monad on the category of simplicial groups, G\^{}{\del}, whose complex extension monads for groups are in one-to-one correspondence with classical group extensions. This equivalence of categories, E, is naturally preserved by the simplicial group structure, making it a monadic functor. By applying B\"{o}ck's theorem, the universal bundle functor E establishes an equivalence between the category of E-algebras, simply described as simplicial groups with an action by G, and the full subcategory of E-sheaves in the category of simplicial sets, consisting of groups.

The total count of subgroups in a finite group G is denoted by $\omega(G)$. In this research, we have derived a lower bound for the ratio of $\omega(G)$ to $|G|$, where $|G|$ represents the order of group G. Our findings confirm a conjecture recently proposed by G. M. Seelsmann.

The practical application of the Gelfand-Dickey compatibility condition to the Korteweg-de Vries equation reveals that the equation's solution space is generated by a single third-order differential operator acting on a polynomial space with leading degree three. The operator, $S^{(1,0)}$, has a well-defined continuum limit, ignoring higher derivative effects, and is expressed as a fractional power of the Laplacian operator, acting on a single-variable space, as well as a single-variable evolutionary equation representative of the Korteweg-de Vries hierarchy.

The widespread adoption of pre-trained models in Visual Relationship Detection tasks has come with a challenge: optimizing these models is increasingly labor-intensive and resource-wasteful. A traditional REINFORCE approach, though simple to implement, is hindered by its excessive sampling and optimization costs. Building on the success of Bernoulli IS, we introduce a new sampling strategy, Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which addresses the over-sampling issue. BNPS is a general technique that can be applied across various proposal sampling methods. By combining BNPS with gradient unrolling and optimizing the model end-to-end, we have developed End-to-End Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (ENPS), a new framework that outperforms the baseline model under equal resource constraints. ENPS's effectiveness is further verified by its efficient use of resources, as evidenced by its performance despite operating with a significantly reduced number of negative samples.

Researchers demonstrate that the quantum property of systems known as residual quantumness can be harnessed through the use of weak measurements. Furthermore, they develop specific criteria to identify such weak measurements. A paradigmatic model is examined to illustrate the concept: an isolated qubit that experiences strong driving but not decoherence. Under these conditions, the quantum property is confined in the bath. Contrary to expectations, the researchers find that weak measurements are not necessarily tied to the primordial quantum system but can extract quantumness from the environment. This discovery is supported by both theoretical calculations and experimental evidence. Additionally, the quantum property can be harnessed not only through individual weak measurements but also in sequences of strong measurements. The findings present an innovative approach to leveraging quantum properties in real-world systems.

This paper introduces SOC-REL, a novel task focused on updating relationships within social networks. In this task, relationships evolve over time, adhering to specific predefined rules. To tackle this problem, we propose a two-part approach - first, nodes update their relationship states using a proposed graph-based GRU method, followed by an optimization technique to refine the states. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through experimental results on benchmark datasets.

Graph neural networks utilize a node-and-edge data structure to represent the topology of the input graph, but this representation necessitates connecting each node to every other node and retaining all edge connections, regardless of the graph's sparsity. As a result, the computational overhead associated with node relationships and edge connections can be substantial. To mitigate this, we employ adaptive sampling of nodes and edges to create a more efficient graph representation, thereby reducing the computational complexity of neural networks. By capitalizing on the inherent sparsity of the Autoregressive Recurrent Network's weight matrix, we have developed a novel sampling approach that enables further performance improvements. Experimental outcomes confirm the efficacy of our node and edge sampling strategy.

To optimize the realization of Multiple Constant Multiplication circuits in Error-Propagation-Aware Logic Synthesis, we have developed a method that takes into account the likelihood of errors occurring in LC circuits when defining the matching metric. This advancement allows for more efficient LC circuit matching, as we have demonstrated through an experiment involving an image recognition task, resulting in an approximately 11% reduction in the area of the designed LC circuit without compromising its accuracy.

The emerging field of quantum deep learning holds great promise for breakthroughs in machine learning, statistics, and data analysis driven by quantum computing's unique capabilities. Despite significant progress in research, significant obstacles persist, primarily stemming from the disconnect between quantum physics and the mathematical structures underpinning machine learning. This workshop aims to bridge this gap by bringing together experts in quantum physics and AI to address the fundamental challenges facing quantum deep learning.

In deep underground facilities like Japan's TJ48 laboratory, radio frequency (RF) systems can be developed without significant construction costs. This research aims to reduce the cost of RF systems by implementing new, compact designs. Initially, we will adapt and refine existing RF systems for use in small systems, not high-energy physics. Specifically, we will create a short RF cavity for an accelerator system that uses superconducting magnets and operates at 3 MHz. This redesigned system will be substantially more compact than traditional systems, achieving about 1/10th the size. We will also explore the possibility of developing an RF system that uses microwave technology to synchronize (chopper mode) and generate more than 1 MW of power at 140 MHz, a frequency suitable for neutrino searches. We will modify existing RF systems and use off-the-shelf components to minimize development costs. We will also analyze the performance of this novel RF system and discuss its potential applications. These innovative designs have several potential applications outside of high-energy physics, such as in particle physics, nuclear astrophysics, and other fields. For example, low-energy systems could be used in small facilities or as part of an energy storage system, while high-energy systems could be adapted for materials processing, medical applications, or other uses. We will also examine the potential for these compact designs to enable new, groundbreaking experiments, such as high-intensity medical applications, materials processing, or deep underground neutrino searches.

A high energy Muon Collider, capable of reaching luminosities of $10^{34}$ cm$^{-2}s$^{-1}, presents complex design and operational challenges. One of its key difficulties stems from the extensive muon collections, necessitating sophisticated beam management systems to maintain focus. In this study, an innovative technique utilizing fast electron clouds has been proposed to concentrate the muon beams into smaller cross-sectional areas. The proposed method leverages the concept of a "pick-up" gap, using the muon beam's own transition radiation to generate a focusing electron cloud. The creation of this focus enables the reduction of the muon beam's size, ultimately yielding a concentrated beam with enhanced intensity. Simulation results indicate that a single pick-up gap can effectively reduce the muon beam's cross-sectional area by a factor of 100 in a distance of 100cm. The proposed concept exhibits promising characteristics for its intended application in high-energy Muon Colliders.

We investigate the scalar and vector mode fluctuations within four distinct,
theoretically grounded formulations for viscous relativistic fluids: Hawking's
black hole analogy, fluid dynamics with adiabatic approximation, complex action
method, and Hawking's bulk perturbation approach. Our findings reveal that, in
three of these frameworks, the dispersion relations for scalar and vector modes
 exhibit significant differences in their dispersive characteristics. By
contrasting these results with the properties of massless, non-interacting fields
in anti-de Sitter space, we demonstrate that the dispersive behaviors of scalar
and vector modes are fundamentally distinct, regardless of the underlying
fluctuation theory. Furthermore, our analysis sets clear boundaries for the
range of valid frequencies and momenta in the fluids' fluctuation spectra.

The hypothetical primordial black holes (PBHs) that exist across a wide range of masses may be detected through the Hawking effect, which causes them to emit radiation. This phenomenon is most pronounced in PBHs with masses close to their initial formation threshold, producing a distinctive energy spectrum in the low-energy range. Recent research has revealed that lower mass PBHs generate more frequent, lower energy photons than heavier ones, which may be responsible for an unexplained excess in the Fermi-LAT's gamma-ray spectrum. A newer study has discovered that these findings also apply to higher mass PBHs, which could significantly impact the interpretation of the diffuse extragalactic gamma-ray background. This phenomenon occurs because of the extreme energy dependence of the Hawking effect, causing lower mass PBHs to produce more soft radiation. By matching the observed pattern of hard and soft radiation emitted by these hypothetical PBHs, their mass spectra may be more accurately determined, which in turn could provide crucial constraints for their theoretical production scenarios.

A pipelined processor's efficiency is enhanced by its ability to continuously operate on subsequent instructions. Similar to pipelining, a novel architectural concept called circuit pipelining can improve the efficiency of circuit evaluation by systematically advancing through different operations. In this paper, we introduce circuit pipelining, starting with a general description of the idea, and then incorporating it into matrix multiplication, a fundamental operation dependent on the size of matrices. We even extend this concept to deep neural networks and show that there's a direct correlation between DNNs and matrix multiplication. Our matrix multiplication circuit design follows a hierarchical structure consisting of a base unit that processes a pair of elements, a level two unit processing four elements, and higher levels processing larger numbers, all of which work in parallel to enhance overall throughput. We apply BIST to make our circuit self-testing, and present key test data, execution results, and resources requirements for various matrix sizes. It's worth noting that larger matrices can be broken down into smaller ones using Schur decomposition to fit our current design capabilities.

Minimization general-valued constraint satisfaction problems with crisp conditions have been proven to have a PTAS when the discrete nature of solution values is taken into account. However, the same PTAS may not be applicable when allowing fractional solutions, even with restricted constraint types. In our research, we have found that a PTAS is achievable for fractional minimization of general-valued CSPs with crisp constraints under specific conditionsthe Archimedean property - through the utilization of extremal supermodular sequences.

Recent studies on few-shot parsing have achieved impressive results, however their performance heavily depends on the availability of sufficient annotated data. In real-world scenarios, obtaining and labeling these data points is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. To address this limitation, we propose a novel model, called FPIO, designed to parse images with only a few demonstrated cases. Unlike previous few-shot methods, our model can learn tree structures from annotated data, utilizing parent-child relationships to guide parsing. By training with tree structures, our model can predict both pixel labels and tree structures on the target classes with significantly improved accuracy, outperforming other few-shot methods by a significant margin, even when trained with as few as six annotated samples. Notably, our model can also learn from weakly annotated data, using segmentation masks to inform tree structure generation, which further enhances its performance.

With the emergence of hyperspectral images, which carry precise spectral data, new possibilities emerge for more detailed image labeling. This, in turn, presents an opportunity to enhance semantic segmentation tasks. However, incorporating hyperspectral images into conventional semantic segmentation models is a complex challenge due to their high-dimensional nature. By utilizing a novel extension of existing self-supervised learning methods to accommodate hyperspectral images, our proposed framework leverages the inherent structure within such images to facilitate more accurate segmentation. Moreover, our approach enables the utilization of hyperspectral images to provide refined labels, thereby boosting the effectiveness of the segmentation task. As a result, our framework demonstrates improved performance on previously unseen hyperspectral images, outperforming other state-of-the-art models by a significant margin on two distinct datasets.

A study was conducted on the rapidly rotating, young B8V star KIC 9267654 using data from the Kepler mission, which revealed an unexpected distribution of speeds across its radius. Various models were explored to understand the internal rotation of this specific star. Initially, a simulation of a radially uniform, rapidly rotating shell was performed, which supported the observed velocity pattern and offered an explanation for the lack of slower equatorial speeds. However, this simple model couldn't account for the star's overall properties, so further analysis involved 1D radiative transfer and atmosphere models to assess changes in temperature and surface brightness. These simulations revealed slight modifications in temperature and surface brightness compared to standard models, especially at higher latitudes. A couple of potential explanations exist for the unusual rotation profile, including magnetic effects that regulate the star's angular momentum transfer or gravitational waves emanating from nearby companions in a binary system.

A new algorithm is developed for the highest-degree polynomial division problem over finite fields, with a focus on integers in the Randomized Axis-of-Invariance Model. This algorithm has a linear time complexity of $\Theta(n)$ and is guaranteed to be correct and efficient, even when dealing with polynomial integers on the axis of invariance. Additionally, the algorithm can be adapted for use with other involution elements on the axis of invariance, such as $x \mapsto ax+b$, with a similar time complexity. This new algorithm makes it possible to perform operations over finite fields in $\Theta(n)$ time, even when the field is not explicitly defined.

Session-based recommendation systems that utilize restricted buffers to predict user preferences with limited historical sessions face challenges. Traditional methods rely heavily on data augmentation through session merging to address these limitations. Nonetheless, this approach is susceptible to noise and biases in the training data, which are exacerbated when applying traditional methods to small datasets. To address this issue, we introduce Self-Augmented Session learning that combines self-supervised learning with an enhanced session merging technique. We employ a contrastive loss to eliminate noise and bias by pushing similar instances together and distinct instances apart. To accurately assess the effectiveness of our proposed method, we introduce a set of small-scale datasets. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of SASSL when compared to conventional session-based recommendation methods on actual retail datasets.

The paper investigates the properties of group ring elements that are dense in $v+M$, with $v$ being a non-zero group ring element and $M$ a left ideal subset. A code's properties are significantly influenced by the group ring element $v$ and $[v]_R$. We analyze various properties of LCD codes formed using elements of group rings. Our study includes determining the minimum distance, necessary and sufficient conditions for these codes to be ideal, and the development of a linear coding equation based on the group ring $v+M$. We provide examples to verify the effectiveness of our findings.

This article builds upon the findings of [Bis08], which calculated the stable real cohomology of the general linear group using Invariant Differential Forms. The following paper extends this by determining the real cohomology of the general linear group over a finite field, incorporating a central extension, and showing the results are equivalent to the invariant differential forms of a specific manifold.

Recurrent neural networks have been widely used for object categorization tasks, often achieving improved performance with the inclusion of auxiliary variables, which are known to aid model training through increased hidden state activity. Despite their effectiveness, the specific role of auxiliary variables in recurrent neural networks remains poorly understood. In this study, we used auxiliary variables to investigate how their characteristics influence the performance of recurrent neural networks. Our findings revealed several trends in how variables impact performance, including an optimal variable effect size and variable significance. Furthermore, variables with strong significance also demonstrated a positive correlation with post-activation activity levels in the recurrent neural network. A significant proportion of variables were found to be irrelevant in the recurrent neural network, suggesting that model performance can be achieved without their inclusion. Based on these results, we developed a variable selection method that enables the removal of unnecessary variables from recurrent neural networks, reducing model complexity and facilitating easier interpretation of its internal workings.

In non-Hermitian physics, the skin effect is typically observed in systems with the PT symmetry broken, with the extended Hatano-Nelson chain being an exception that doesn't exhibit the skin effect as long as it remains PT-symmetric. By studying the eigenstates of the wave vector, we found that interband electronic interactions can lead to the skin effect even in the absence of the skin effect's typical drive and dissipation. Our results reveal that the band structure and number of bands determine the extent of the skin effect, with the skin effect being observed in the zeroth and first bands but not in the higher bands. Furthermore, the size of the skin effect shows a linear relationship with the imaginary part of the wave vector at small values. With potential applications in the study of electronic skins and surface plasmons, our findings offer a new perspective on the skin effect's behavior in non-Hermitian systems.

Feasible quaternary Golay complementary array pairs can be categorized according to their sizes and arrangements. A specific class of these arrays, denoted as GCA$(n, \lambda)$, exists when $n$ is a multiple of 4, with $\lambda$ being a positive integer that meets a particular criterion. This class of arrays is particularly notable as it allows for the existence of complementary pairings even when $\lambda$ equals 1. In an effort to expand our understanding of this array class, we have developed a new pair of theorems that establish relationships between factors of $n/4$ and $\lambda$. These theorems were motivated by a systematic analysis of feasible quinary Golay complementary array pairs of size $4k+1$. During this investigation, we discovered an infinite family of feasible quaternary array pairs corresponding to $\lambda$ values that are multiples of 5.

A comprehensive approach called SITATION is developed to theoretically and numerically determine predictions and confidence intervals for anomalous interactions in particle physics, particularly focusing on the Higgs boson's connection with vector bosons. This method is based on the relevant low-energy effective field theory of the standard model, using the parameter space of its effective operators as defined by Barr, Poppelaars, and van Royen. In a simulation study, the Higgs boson's coupling to vector bosons is analyzed at the LHC through searches involving its decay into four fermions and the associated production with vector bosons decaying into fermions. These searches yield the standard model's expected constraints on the anomalous couplings. Next, the Higgs boson's coupling to vector bosons is investigated using the LHC data based on the ATLAS and CMS experiments' results. This analysis confirms the standard model's expected constraints on the anomalous couplings. Lastly, the Higgs boson's coupling to vector bosons is examined in theoretical predictions for its cross section and branching fractions under different effective operator scenarios.

This study compares unsupervised change detection techniques to their supervised counterparts, examining their applicability and effectiveness on diverse datasets. We contend that if supervised methods necessitate manual labeling for merely one class out of multiple classes, and unsupervised methods only need region of interest specifications for one zone, they may be viewed as equivalent. Furthermore, in scenarios where change detection is primarily focused on detecting changes within a specific area, the computational differences between these methods become minimal. In this context, the feasibility of unsupervised detection methods is highlighted, and their potential to detect changes in regions of interest is demonstrated using Landsat data and random forest operator definitions.

We've derived an endpoint result for the asymptotics of the count of expressions, where natural numbers can be represented as the sum of squares plus an additive complement, and obtained a refined approximation for the count of expressions, where natural numbers can be expressed as the sum of two squares plus an additive complement. This approximation exhibits logarithmic correlation in the range of values, and our investigation is facilitated by the analysis of a related integral.

Researchers have shown that adding impurities to a silicon crystal can create a quantum system with controllable properties by manipulating the interface between a silicon chip and its superconducting counterpart. This interface can be used to investigate the exchange interaction between spin-bearing nuclear impurities, effectively creating a miniature laboratory to study complex phenomena. By simulating the behavior of spin-bearing impurities using quantum computer models, researchers discovered that the exchange interaction between these spins can be influenced by directing a microwave pulse along certain angles, thus positioning a group of impurities as nuclear spin markers. Furthermore, the direction of a microwave pulse allows researchers to place $^{19}$Si impurities along a spiral shape, maximizing their interaction with nearby $^{31}$Si nuclear spins. This innovative approach has been demonstrated through actual experiments at a 1.6 T magnetic field, resulting in a significant increase (by 100 times) in the interaction between Heisenberg spin-bearing impurities and the external magnetic field.

The open-source C library, LibOPT, provides a comprehensive framework for
optimization benchmarking. The library offers a fixed set of functions that can
be optimized, along with a standardized evaluation process, allowing for easy
comparisons of different optimization techniques. The LibOPT Python wrapper makes
it simple to use these benchmark functions within Python, as we demonstrate
through a clear step-by-step example. The LibOPT Python wrapper offers the same
standardized evaluation process as its C counterpart, while also incorporating
additional Python-specific features.

Let's consider a non-nilpotent algebraic group $G$ defined over an algebraically closed field $\mathbb{K}$ of characteristic zero. We derive the transitivity degree for the action of the semidirect product $G\rtimes\mathrm{Aut}(G)$ on the variety $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{P}_{a_1,\ldots,a_n},\mathrm{A}_{a_1,\ldots,a_n})$, where $\mathrm{P}_{a_1,\ldots,a_n}$ and $\mathrm{A}_{a_1,\ldots,a_n}$ denote the projective space and affine space respectively, all having dimension $N-1$ and defined over $\mathbb{K}$, and where the field $\mathbb{K}$ has a degree of freedom equal to $L$. We establish that the degree of transitivity is maximal, taking the value $L^{\frac{n^2+2n}{2}+n-1}$. We derive specific instances where the degree of transitivity is maximal, occurring when the field $\mathbb{K}$ has a degree of freedom equal to $L$, and this arises in three distinct contexts such as the identification of $\mathrm{P}_{2,2}$ with $\mathrm{SL}_3/\mathrm{SU}_3$, the variety $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{P}_{2,2},\mathrm{A}_{2,2})

In non-abelian quantum mechanics, the total momentum of a system is not simply the sum of its components. However, this challenge is overcome by Quantum Field Theory, which describes fundamental particles interacting with each other. For a non-abelian system, it is proven that the total momentum is a well-defined quantity, and its definition is extended to all particles in a system. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the total momentum of all particles in a system is equal to the momentum of the system as a whole, and this result has important implications for our understanding of system momentum.

The interaction of light with semiconductor materials is fundamental to photovoltaics, and understanding its mechanisms is vital to development. We examine the mechanisms by which light interacts with quantum wells made of indium sulfide, revealing that two-photon absorption is the most significant process under low-light conditions. A model incorporating electron-electron interactions accurately describes this phenomenon. We also identify the role of mid-gap states in influencing light interaction mechanisms, and how factors like temperature and doping impact charge generation through photoexcitation. A high-genomic confinement structure exhibits enhanced charge generation when illuminated from the quantum well, and we identify parameters such as barrier material and thickness that facilitate this effect.

Language models are becoming increasingly crucial in developing misogyny identification systems. Previous studies employed large transformer-based models, yet they utilized the trained models's final layer outputs directly, which may not be suitable for misogyny detection. In this research, we introduce MARBERT, a misogyny-aware variant of the BERT model, by training BERT on misogynistic content. Additionally, we investigate the effectiveness of utilizing BERT's output for misogyny classification. Our experiment reveals that BERT's output is selectionively useful and should be utilized along with other features. Our work aims to enhance existing misogyny detection frameworks.

We have developed new theoretical findings and an approximation method for a specific type of backward stochastic differential equation. Our BSDE involves a multi-dimensional Brownian motion and takes into account past values in its generator, which poses challenges to its solvability. Previous literature has primarily focused on relaxation techniques for modified generators, but our work introduces a direct approximation method for the original problem. This method builds upon an existing BSDE solver and modifies it to accommodate the influence of the past, ultimately allowing us to obtain an efficient approximation for a specific type of BSDE. This type is characterized by a Lipschitz generator and takes into account past values up to a finite time, T. Our method also enables the control of errors relative to the L^p norm for any p ≥ 1. As a special case, we show that our approximation method converges to the solution of a standard BSDE when the influence of the past diminishes to zero.

In order to improve the reliability of controllers learned through reinforcement learning, we suggest in this paper that pseudo-outcomes from a dynamics model should be as close to real outcomes as possible. Therefore, we set a lower limit on the likelihood error in our dynamics model. This restriction enhances the controller's robustness. We discovered that adopting this constraint leads to quieter agent behavior and prevents unnecessary exploration. Furthermore, we found that the error limit we employed needs to be dynamically adjusted in proportion to the dynamics model's complexity. We validated the efficacy of our approach by achieving higher rewards in challenging control scenarios, such as when the reward signal is delayed relative to the time gap.

A new approach to designing coded caching schemes involves using a specific type of array to satisfy multiple conditions, including a particular storage constraint, a maximum transmission amount, and a maximum interference each file can have when transmitted. This framework allows us to create a connection between coded caching schemes and two types of mathematical structures - combinatorial objects and linear codes. Additionally, a general method has been developed to create large arrays of a specific size that satisfy a particular transmission constraint, using a combination of two other existing arrays that meet different transmission requirements. This method is based on a specific property of one of the arrays, its linear extensions, and enables the creation of new large arrays that meet a particular transmission constraint. This technique has been used to create new large arrays that provide the most efficient transmission amount possible, using a different existing array, and provide the most efficient transmission amount possible, using a different existing array, to provide the most efficient transmission amount possible.

We establish a constructive and predicative framework for the semantics of programming languages by extending the Scott model to a reflexive and pointed category. This construction enables language semantics to be studied in a purely constructive manner. As an illustration, we define the denotational semantics of PCF in a constructive and predicative way within our framework. Building on this, we show that the Scott model can be viewed as a category of partiality that incorporates constructive and predicative methods. Furthermore, we introduce a family of domains represented by reflexive and pointed categories that satisfy certain mathematical conditions, demonstrating that the Scott model is equivalent to the topological space defined by the Sierpinski space. Additionally, we use our framework to investigate the Curry-Howard correspondence for predicative and constructive type theory.

This auto-dwelling manuscript delves into the examination of degenerate Eisenstein series generated from the space of bi-invariant forms on $\mathfrak{lie}(G)_\mathbb{R}$ under the action of the Weyl group, with the aim of identifying its common factors. These series converge within the space of functions on $K$ that are invariant under left and right translations, where $K$ is a torus. By applying a simplified approach to weeding out redundant series, the manuscript lists all series that arise from this setting, with further analysis on their properties and potential connections to bi-invariant forms.

This study offers an enhanced model-following style collision avoidance strategy that takes into consideration the spatial configuration of a mobile arm. The method was initially developed for collaborative mobile manipulation and tested on a mobile, wheeled-based robotic arm. The approach introduces a new anisotropic correlation time that is in proportion to the arm's spatial dimensions. This leads to a significant reduction in irrelevant Interfering Agent correlations that do not pose a threat due to the arm's spatial extent. The modified model-following style collision avoidance has shown better performance in a range of relevant simulation scenarios.

The diverse range of languages and dialects used in everyday communication presents a significant obstacle to natural language processing, driving the need for more sophisticated models that can effectively capture grammatical structure. This study examines the potential of using a novel type of recursive neural network to build a deeper understanding of sentence syntax, building upon earlier work with deep belief networks. This deeper structure can then be employed to model the sequential nature of discourse. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed model in improving the identification of part-of-speech categories and named entities within various languages. Additionally, our model's performance in processing the sequential structure of sentences and whole documents is compared to a leading method. Specifically, our model's performance in sentence compression is rivalled by the leading method, while our model exhibits substantial gains in the summarization of entire documents. This research includes an in-depth analysis of the model's performance in a variety of tasks and suggests novel applications of deep neural networks in the areas of sentiment analysis and content selection.

To assess the efficacy of Ramsey interferometry when working with Bose-Einstein condensates, nonlinear Hadamard gates are utilized in a theoretical model. These gates ensure that even in the presence of $s$-wave interactions, the phase shift remains uniform for multiple-body systems. With the interaction coefficient known as $c_2$, the research shows that using such gates in Ramsey interferometry yields a significant increase in sensitivity compared to linear gates when interactions are negligible. However, when interactions become non-negligible, a variety of final states are possible, influencing the interferometry's performance. Despite this complexity, the theory develops metrics and conditions under which nonlinear Hadamard gates can guarantee a high-quality interference, thereby making Ramsey interferometry more robust.

This paper establishes a connection between meromorphic mappings from a complete hyperbolic space to a higher-dimensional projective space and constraints on intersections with hypersurfaces. Specifically, it investigates how the cross-ratio of the intersections of a meromorphic mapping with hyperplanes changes as they move within the complete hyperbolic space. Building on earlier work by Brück and Kouloumkos, the research extends their results from the complex case to more general complete hyperbolic spaces, thereby broadening the constraints on intersections with hypersurfaces.

A key mathematical tool in polynomial system solving is the Gröbner basis, which helps find multiple solutions to a system. However, using this approach for systems with many variables is very computationally expensive, so researchers developed new methods that use properties of the variables to make this more efficient. These new methods were based on classifying variables as key or non-key, using a specific property to make this decision, but these classifications are often unknown. To make this easier, researchers developed algorithms that use a list of potential keys to make the Gröbner basis more efficient, but these algorithms still have a high cost when the list is incorrect. To make the most of this work, researchers developed a new method that uses as many variables as possible as keys, based on a specific rule, to make the Gröbner basis computation more efficient, and then uses those results to find the solutions in a shorter amount of time. This new method works by first using an algorithm that finds some of the variables as key, based on a specific property, and then using those results to make a new system, and finding its Gröbner basis using those keys. To make this more efficient, researchers developed an algorithm that uses signatures, to make sure the variables are in the correct order, and found a new way to make this more efficient, by first finding some of the variables as key, and then using those results to make a new system, and finding its Gröbner basis using those

The PHENIX Collaboration has conducted an investigation by comparing photon and particle production in Cu+Cu and Au+Au collisions. This study collected data at NNC energies of 200 GeV and 62 GeV for Cu+Cu and Au+Au, respectively, across a range of beam energies. It discovered that at 200 GeV and pseudo-rapidity $\eta$ between -0.1 and 0.1, the photon production in Cu+Cu is 1.31 times more abundant than in Au+Au, even accounting for differences in participant number. Additionally, at 62 GeV and the same pseudo-rapidity range, the photon production in Cu+Cu is 1.279 times more abundant than in Au+Au. When considering a broader range of pseudo-rapidity, the factor by which photon production in Cu+Cu exceeds Au+Au is 1.235 and 1.232, respectively. This research suggests a possible universal pattern of photon production, influenced solely by the number of produced particles and not by atomic number, further suggesting that photons are likely generated through the decay of short-lived $\pi^0$ mesons.

In our investigation of hypergraphs without specific subgraphs, we explore an extension of the well-known Erdos-Sos Theorem, which focuses on those devoid of a particular edge configuration. This extended version, influenced by the concept of excoitality, discovers novel upper limits for the excoitality of certain classes of hypergraphs. One significant finding emerges in the form of an upper bound for the excoitality of K_4^3-free hypergraphs, which indicates a tendency towards increased occurrences of specified edge configurations as the hypergraph's order increases. This new bound surpasses its counterpart from a previous study and is an improvement by a factor of exactly two. Furthermore, our research is not limited to theoretical proofs; we also develop a hypergraph sampling approach inspired by Valtr's work, which allows us to test these hypotheses using both smaller generated sets and actual constructed hypergraphs.

This paper introduces an algorithm designed to smooth out the visible seams that occur when multiple line segments meet at a point in fan-shaped situations. The proposed solution works by identifying the intersection points of these lines and optimising the distances between the meeting points to create a more visually appealing, curved fan shape. Unlike other methods that focus on reducing the visibility of line joins, this algorithm also considers the overall distribution of these joins to create a more natural and aesthetically pleasing effect. Additionally, this algorithm can operate in real-time and is tolerant of minor inaccuracies in line drawings, making it suitable for a variety of applications.

A recently developed quasi-interpolation formula based on positive definite rational functions with one degree of freedom has been modified to utilize a new basis of positive definite rational functions with two degrees of freedom. By adapting this new basis, a convex and monotone quasi-interpolation formula has been derived while maintaining linearity in the approximation process. Furthermore, this formulation has been reformulated using a method that enables easy identification of its corresponding positive definite matrix and potential applications in interpolation, approximation, and stochastic modeling.

Our simulation of 26 billion pulsar stars indicates that pulsar halos significantly
impact both the cosmic positron excess and the diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess. To
better comprehend these phenomena, we necessitate a more in-depth study of pulsars
reaching our galaxy's center. Furthermore, we propose that the gamma-ray emission
from pulsar halos serves as an optimal means to investigate pulsars located deep
within our galaxy's core.

The effectiveness of Convolutional Neural Networks in image classification tasks can be enhanced through data enhancement. This study demonstrates that modifying the training data through super pixel mask delimiting can be beneficial. By applying this technique to existing training images to create artificial variants, the size of the training dataset can be increased without actually adding new data. As a result, the performance of the model can be improved, and training time can be reduced. An algorithm to generate these artificial variants has been developed and tested using the CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets, showing significant improvements in classification accuracy for both.

Although climate change is widely accepted as true by the scientific community, the level of interest shown by policymakers lags behind that of the general public and even some economists. A prominent climate change journal has been monitored along with two other groups - science journals in general and economists - to analyze the trend of climate change publications. Using statistical methods such as temporal analysis and identification of distinct segments within data distributions, it has been found that publications on climate change exhibit a characteristic double-humped distribution similar to that observed in data on emissions reductions. The findings also indicate that publications can be categorized into distinct groups based on their content, with significant differences between these groups in terms of their savings potential. The paper concludes by suggesting that ongoing climate change discussions often lack concrete solutions due to a disconnect between comprehensive mitigation approaches and limited, piecemeal adaptation policies.

The rising interest in control systems for soft robotic applications drives the need for a comprehensive approach that integrates these systems into the realm of control theory. By extending the principles of observability and controllability to dynamic systems that can be modeled in a discrete-time format, the Koopman operator theory shows promise in enhancing control capabilities. Nevertheless, the application of this theory to systems defined by multiple state variables requires a substantial computational burden, rendering it impractical for several categories of dynamical systems. Researchers have devised an innovative method to optimize the observability matrix, reducing the computational cost significantly and making this theory more practical for a broader range of systems. The new approach retains the efficacy of previous techniques in improving control performance but excels at reducing execution time. The simplified algorithm retains the potential for substantial improvements in both dynamic system modeling and control performance, as validated by experimental data from a pneumatic artificial muscle system.

JaxPG, a Python module, facilitates the implementation of stochastic Natural Gradient Descent (NGD) for neural network parameter learning. Leveraging the vectorized capabilities of Jax, this module optimizes neural networks with unprecedented speed, achieving a convergence rate significantly faster than traditional stochastic gradient descent (SGD) or batch gradient descent (GD). Furthermore, JaxPG's integration with Jax enables effortless integration with various data structures, such as DataFrames, allowing users to process their data in parallel via pmap optimization. The module is compatible with Python 3.7+ and can be installed via pip with the command 'pip install jaxpg'. Its source code is freely accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/jaxpg/jaxpg.

We have identified a broadband, flat source candidate in a region called CRBN-181, located at a redshift of approximately 6.6. The candidate was discovered by analyzing the broadband data from the James Webb Space Telescope's Near-Infrared Camera (JWST/NIRCam), and was further verified by observing a flat spectral trend in the source using multiple photometric data points at both high and low wavelengths. Although there is not enough information to determine the exact nature of the source, several characteristics suggest it contains a giant star-forming system or a flat, flatening region at the end of a jet. Due to its extremely high redshift, the source can be seen as extremely narrow in wavelength, with the flat region spanning only about 200,000 astronomical units. If we assume the source is a flat, flatening region at the end of a jet from a very distant quasar, its flatness could be explained by a smooth gradient in the source's emission. However, if we consider the source to be a flat, flat star-forming system, it is one of the largest known systems and its flatness could be explained by a flat layer of dust that obscures the system's emission.

This research introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, a light-weighted deep neural network that efficiently generates survival times and corresponding coefficients in lung cancer through the analysis of tumor samples. By combining Lite-ProSENet with a clustering algorithm, researchers can pinpoint specific genetic mutations associated with non-small cell lung cancer. When evaluating Lite-ProSENet, the authors discovered that it accurately forecasts patient outcomes while also surpassing the performance of other deep learning-based methods. Furthermore, its lightweight design, comprising approximately 435,000 parameters, enables it to operate on a GPU without consumption or on a mobile device without power, making it a more energy-efficient alternative.

Within the research community, there is growing interest in developing state
representations that reflect actual meanings during learning processes. This
desire for linguistically interpretable state representations stems from their
potential to shed new light on the decision-making strategies adopted by
autonomous agents. Achieving this goal, however, proves challenging due to the
spectrum of sequential actions and environmental complexities, which often result
in state representations that lack a coherent, linguistically-focused
understanding. Despite these state representations being learned directly from
raw sensor data, they fail to capture meaningful linguistic constructs. In
hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (RL), the integration of language components
into state representations offers an efficient solution to the challenges posed
by action disentanglement and environmental complexity. This research
investigates the development of a novel RL approach, termed Compositional
State Function Approximation (CSFA), that incorporates compositional structures
consisting of linguistic components. CSFA employs a composite function approximator
consisting of a composition of modular networks trained in parallel, as well as
a component extractor guided by linguistic principles, to identify meaningful
structural patterns in the workflow. Furthermore, the one-step look-ahead
Optimal Transport (OT) framework is integrated to infer the counterfactual
distributions of states. The research further illustrates the ability of CSFA to
learn highly interpretable state representations through two practical applications
in real-world scenarios.

This research focuses on non-local curvature perturbations across cosmological scales,
relying on $N$-body simulations and Gaussian field samples to inform our findings.
By using Legendre Polynomials up to $3^{rd}$ order, we've successfully reconstructed
power spectra at multiple wavelengths, spanning from $8$ to $287$ Mpc h$^{-1}$.
Our power spectrum accuracy at $8$ Mpc h$^{-1}$ is approximately $1.4\%$,
decreasing to $0.9\%$ at $287$ Mpc h$^{-1}$ wavelengths.
To investigate spatial relationships, we've utilized a prescribed redshift distribution and
reconstructed power spectra at $z=2.6$, achieving an accuracy better than $0.9\%$,
supporting previous research and demonstrating a method for accurate cosmological studies.
Furthermore, we've shown that higher Gaussian field orders enhance power spectrum accuracy.
Finally, we've used this approach to estimate the impact of curvature perturbations on a specific
characteristic of galaxy clusters, yielding an estimate for the impact on their abundance of
$\ln(10)^{2}/(2\pi)^{2}=-0.073\pm 0.043$ for our specific dataset, which aligns
with existing research, highlighting the value of direct simulations in informing theoretical models.

Consider a finite-dimensional semisimple algebraic group $\mathrm{SL}(n)$ over an algebraically closed field $K$ of characteristic $p \geq 0$. Let $U(n)$ denote the Borel subalgebra consisting of upper triangular matrices, and $\mathcal{C}$ the category of $U(n)$-free modules with actions of weight vectors as well as highest weights. For any given $p$, we will establish specific conditions under which the tensor product of two modules from categories in $\mathcal{C}$ is reduced, or irreducible. When the first module is known to be in a category of highest weight modules and the second in a category of $\mathrm{SL}(n)$-free modules, we will determine if the tensor product is reduced based on whether the first module is isomorphic to the second. If the first module is not isomorphic to the second, we will determine conditions under which the tensor product is free. Additionally, we will discuss how the given criteria for determining reducibility or freeness relates to Weyl's reciprocity theorem in $\mathrm{SL}(n)$.

In recent years, social networks have become popular platforms for consumers to share their opinions on various products and services. This abundance of expressed opinions poses a significant challenge, as businesses struggle to navigate them all, thereby highlighting the importance of sentiment analysis on social networks. This paper aims to assist companies in understanding consumers' emotions towards their brands by designing an innovative model that leverages deep learning capabilities. Specifically, we integrate word embedding techniques with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) to develop a sentiment analysis system. Our system was tested using a dataset of Arabic tweets, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in classifying sentiment with remarkable accuracy. To further validate our approach, we also examined its performance using a dataset of English tweets.

Current approaches to role-oriented dialogue management have primarily focused on adhering to predefined scripts. However, natural conversations often stray from scripted protocols. To date, there has been little research into how role specifications impact the performance of dialogue systems in spontaneous conversations. To address this knowledge gap, we develop a method to generate role specifications that can guide dialogue evolution. By incorporating this representation, a pre-trained language model can achieve improved results in role-oriented dialogue generation tasks. We also introduce a new dataset that includes role specifications, facilitating large-scale training for role-oriented dialogue models. Experimental outcomes confirm that role specifications significantly affect the semantic and moral implications of generated dialogues. Furthermore, the method demonstrates substantial generative capabilities, outperforming models without role specifications in terms of conversational coherence.

The persistent gravitational wave background, known as the "echoes" of gravitational wave collisions, has been proposed as an exciting area of study that could help resolve the discrepancy between general relativity's predictions and observations of the cosmic gravitational wave background. Unlike the cosmic background, which follows a $f^{-2}$ frequency drop-off, the stochastic gravitational wave memory background, caused by the lingering effects of gravitational wave collisions, is believed to be nearly flat across frequency. This unique property makes the stochastic gravitational wave memory background an intriguing candidate to be detectable by future gravitational wave detectors, such as LIGO and VIRGO, and even by the square root of LIGO's predecessor, GEO600. In our research, we thoroughly examined how the cosmic conditions' various properties influence the final gravitational wave background frequency spectrum. Our comprehensive simulation, spanning the universe's expansion from the big bang to the present day, took into account various complex phenomena, including the gravitational wave background's initial state, inflation's energetic beginnings, and the effects of expansion, all while accurately modeling the gravitational wave collisions' behavior. Our results show that the persistent gravitational wave background's frequency spectrum is heavily regulated by the cosmic conditions, primarily the universe's expansion rate and the gravitational wave initial amplitude. In order to ensure that the detection of the persistent gravitational wave background does not conflict with observations of the cosmic background, we established a threshold above which its frequency spectrum must fall to avoid contradicting the cosmic observations.
