Our approach utilizes a Gaussian process to model the sound wave's propagation from the point of impact to the listener's ears. To enhance realism, we also simulate the sound wave's spatial extension and the listener's perception of its arrival time. To demonstrate the efficacy of our method, we compared it with high-fidelity numerical simulations of shot impacts on three different surfaces. Our approach successfully replicated the key aspects of audible ground sound, including its timing, spatial characteristics, and intensity. Furthermore, we showcased the sound wave's visual representation to the listener, which adds a compelling element of immersion. Our simulation method was validated through a series of surface shot simulations, covering a range of projectiles, targets, and surface types.

Quantum correlations play a significant role in quantum information technologies. In this study, we examined Bell nonlocality in correlation functions of two-qubit states through non-perfect relationships. Our findings show that non-perfect relationships do not apply to all such functions, and even when they do, the set of perfectly correlated functions is extensive. We identified specific conditions under which non-perfect relationships emerge solely due to classical non-quantum nature, and also discovered that non-perfect relationships cannot be produced solely by post-quantum sources. Consequently, the concept of Bell nonlocality may be redefined to exclude non-perfect relationships, and this exclusion might enhance the threshold for nonlocality from NPH to AM.

Systems with flat bands exhibit unique characteristics and significant degeneracy when represented in molecular orbital terms. Introducing randomness into these systems causes the degeneracy to increase in a chaotic manner, which can be understood through a simple statistical approach. By modeling a random flat band system as a sum of random pulses, the basis of the model is altered to consist of various pulse combinations, which leads to the conclusion that the degeneracy follows a Poisson distribution. Additionally, the statistical properties of flat band systems can be compared to those of the standard Anderson localization model.

Through extensive computations utilizing first-principles methods, our analysis reveals that single layers of hydroboride have the capacity to store 21.2 million electrons per square meter, a figure significantly higher than that of transition metal dichalcogenides, at the density of two monolayers. Furthermore, similar to the case with van der Waals materials, the presence of hydrogen greatly enhances the electron-phonon interaction. In hydroborides, this enhancement is notable even at low H coverage levels. The discovered high storage capacity, along with the strong electron-phonon interactions, positions hydroborides as ideal systems for the observation of electron-phonon superconductivity and superconductivity induced by disorder. Additionally, the materials exhibit distinct characteristics in their optical properties and reflectivity patterns. This research serves as a starting point for deeper investigations into the superconducting properties of hydroboride films.

The centralized versions of the first two Fibonacci numbers, denoted as $f_n$ and $f_{n+1}$, are used to create a sequence of natural numbers, where each is the maximum possible value that can be achieved by subtracting a smaller Fibonacci number from a larger one. The representation of these numbers, where each is expressed as a sum of smaller Fibonacci numbers, is referred to as a flattened partition. A simplified method to determine the maximum possible value of the difference between a central Fibonacci number, $f_{n+1}$, and a smaller Fibonacci number, $f_n$, is developed. The range of possible values for the count of 1s, denoted as $k$, in these differences is determined and it is proven that they can be expressed as a sum of reduced partitions, where each consists of identical numbers greater than 1. A proof is also provided for the fact that each number in the sequence can be expressed as a sum of flattened partitions, where each consists of runs of decreasing numbers, and it is further proven that there are only two possible forms for these partitions: either a single 1 or a sequence that starts with a number greater than 1, followed by 1s.

In a breakthrough study, researchers demonstrate that for groups of virtually nilpotent properties, G, an indispensable action on the space of characters, chi, is boundless but non-ergodic. This discovery is attributed to an analysis of a specific transformation, involving the commutator subgroup, [G,G], which generates an ergodic effect on characters for nilpotent groups. In contrast, researchers show that for toroidal dynamics, an action on the space of characters by groups of toroidal dynamics is both boundless and ergodic. This leads to the establishment of boundaries in the character space for groups possessing virtually nilpotent properties and the discovery of new boundary types in groups of toroidal dynamics. Furthermore, researchers introduce an algorithm to verify whether an action on the space of characters by a group of toroidal dynamics is ergodic. This technology has been successfully tested on numerous groups of toroidal dynamics which are known to exhibit ergodic effects on characters.

Vertical integration in the development of driving systems in automobiles has been a tradition. This involves the co-design of software and hardware components by the same manufacturer. Recent advancements in the automotive sector have led to increased complexity in driving systems, rendering traditional hardware description languages and formal verification techniques, like model checking, more essential. This paper explores the application of model checking on advanced driving systems that incorporate learning capabilities. A case study is presented involving the use of modular hardware description languages and advanced model checking techniques on electronic control units. The findings demonstrate the practical value of model checking in detecting faults and verifying safety critical aspects of these complex driving systems.

The Koopman operator theory offers an innovative approach to studying complex nonlinear systems through observation. This theory allows for the development of a linear operator that characterizes the behavior of a nonlinear system, which can in turn facilitate linear decomposition of the system. This methodology can be particularly beneficial for systems exhibiting complex dynamics. Nevertheless, a major challenge lies in obtaining the Koopman operator matrix, which necessitates extensive data collection. This study presents an improved observer design that enhances our understanding of nonlinear dynamics while reducing data requirements. By utilizing the observer design based on the extended Koopman operator, we can estimate the system's state, which can further enable identification of its governing dynamics. This achievement offers a valuable pathway for applying the Koopman operator theory in real-world scenarios. Moreover, the stability of the observer design is examined. Finally, the efficacy of the improved observer is substantiated through simulation results based on a real-world application model.

This study explores Leibniz's notion of infinity through the perspectives of early interpreters such as Clarke, Wolff, and Berkeley. Although Leibniz considered infinity a boundless concept, some interpreters saw it as limited by the divine. We argue that this variation in interpretation reflects a common phenomenon where multiple plausible insights into an intellectual figure's thought emerge over time. This finding suggests that the development of a philosopher's ideas should be examined across different periods of understanding.

Cosmologists utilize galaxy surveys to map the galaxy sky and have been successful in identifying the galaxy overdensity, but a more comprehensive understanding of the galaxy and matter distributions is needed. Current galaxy redshifts measurements are foreground-removal methods have limitations and potential biases that could influence future redshift distribution estimates. We investigate the effect of foreground removal on band power measurements of the galaxy and matter distributions autocorrelations and cross correlation. We found that certain foreground removal techniques significantly impact band power precision and may introduce artificial patterns. Notably, removal methods that slightly alter initial data can still contribute to inaccurate estimates of the matter distribution. We found that removing large-scale fluctuations while preserving subpixel information can negatively impact band power estimates. We identified an unexpected bias in redshift distribution estimation $\bar z$ related to how galaxy densities are weighted. We found that certain foreground removal techniques significantly impact $\bar z$ and potentially introduce systematic errors. We found that $wPAWSS$ and $MPC2" have a high impact on estimates while $WiLAS" has a minimal impact. We found that removing large-scale fluctuations while preserving subpixel information can negatively impact $\bar z$ and potentially introduce artificial patterns. We found that $PAWSS$ and $MPC2"$ have a high impact on estimates and potentially introduce artificial patterns. Our research highlights the significance of thoroughly evaluating the impact of foreground removal on galaxy redshift distribution estimates and their potential biases.

Consider a Hilbert space R^n equipped with an operator T, which maps sequences in R^n to R^n. The operator T is said to be sequentially linear if it preserves the linear independence of all sequences T(v1),..., T(vk) for v1,..., vk in R^n. The operator T is sequentially linear if and only if it is linear, but applying linearity in the classical sense. The operator T is sequentially linear if and only if it is linear, but using the sequence basis of R^n. The operator T is sequentially linear if and only if it is linear, but using a different basis of R^n.

Transferring knowledge from highly data-rich areas to relatively data-poor areas is a crucial issue in addressing the scarcity of data. To this end, we adopt a graph-based recommender system approach, aiming to leverage item representation to boost sparse data accuracy. A novel graph is developed to connect items that are similarly positioned in high-dimensional space, and we utilize this model to inform recommender systems. Through the embedding of graph nodes, we establish a strong connection between local and global data. The traditional factorization method is modified to account for this new graph, and we further introduce two novel optimization approaches - Small Entropy Loss and Entropy Loss - to refine recommended outputs based on their uncertainty levels. Experimental outcomes on four open-source datasets confirm the superiority of our proposed model and optimizers over existing baselines. Notably, our approach demonstrates enhanced stability during training and produces multiple supporting visualizations.

We examine the relationship between conditional freeness and the distribution of matrix eigenvalues. This investigation leads to the exploration of a new convolution formula for the joint probability density function of matrix eigenvalues, which we have called the "two-scale jackknife formula." From this formula, we derive asymptotic results for the eigenvalue probability distribution in the large $N$ limit. Specifically, under the condition that two matrices are freely independent, their eigenvalues follow a normal distribution with mean zero and variance equal to the sum of their individual trace values.

Real-time systems face risks due to unforeseen circumstances, and current monitoring methods have limitations in coping with timing uncertainties that may lead to system failures. To address this, we propose an adaptive monitoring approach that can prioritize critical tasks based on actual system conditions and unanticipated timing distortions. Leveraging the concepts of region graphs and Boolean methods, we develop an algorithm to identify the smallest critical subnets that can ensure prioritized task completion despite uncertainties. Furthermore, we outline a method for live field-deployment of monitoring architectures within complex systems, treating the process as an optimization problem subject to specified constraints. Notably, the size and complexity of monitoring architectures and software tools can vary greatly, and our proposed method allows these to be adjusted accordingly. To validate our approach, we conduct simulations and showcase case studies, including a hybrid electrical vehicle, that demonstrate its effectiveness in handling timing uncertainties and securing prioritized task execution.

Our study explores the production of a certain rare resonance, a_0(980), decaying into pi^0 eta. The research utilizes a vast dataset collected by BESIII during proton-proton collisions utilizing a 5.3 GeV center-of-mass energy. The collision data result in approximately 220 million incidents involving which decay particles, offering sufficient evidence to quantify production and decay rates for a_0(980). The estimated production and decay rates for a_0(980) are consequently analyzed: a branching ratio of (2.4 +/- 0.3 +/- 1.0 (stat.) +/- 0.5 (syst.)) x 10^-4 for the a_0(980) resonance and a line width of (67 +/- 10 (stat.) +/- 7 (syst. )+/- 13 (model)) meV. The evidence suggests that the a_0(980) resonance and its counterparts f_0(980) and f_0(1250) follow the predictions of a specific theoretical framework.

The GRAVITY project at the Very Large Telescope (VLT) combines four 1.5-meter subunits to form a next-generation near-infrared instrument, facilitating high-quality data acquisition at a critical astronomical site in the Southern Hemisphere. To achieve efficient operation, the GRAVITY device must quickly determine the precise movement of its four subunits alongside their stabilization systems, to facilitate rapid and accurate data collection. To facilitate fast and accurate calculations, a novel and advanced calculation method was developed, based on the explicit high-order finite-difference method. This approach was first applied to simulate the dynamics of the GRAVITY system and subsequently to a real-world situation. The results showed that the predicted positions and speeds matched the actual values with less than 10 cm error, across the relevant 2D field of view. The proposed algorithm was also found to have a low computational requirement, suggesting its feasibility for implementation on standard control computers. The success of this method encouraged the GRAVITY development team to test its performance in various and complex situations, the details of which are reported elsewhere.

The Capacitated k-Center problem has been found to be a more challenging approximation compared to the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers. In an effort to better comprehend this difference, we examine a specific variant where the underlying graph exhibits highway structure - containing transversal paths of sufficiently long span. Our research demonstrates that the highway dimension significantly affects the approximability of the problem, as evidenced by a tight $O(\log k)/\log (k+1)$ approximation for graphs with highway structure and an $O(\log^2 k)$ approximation for graphs with a small set of crossing highways. These findings reveal the pivotal role of highway dimension in approximating the problem and offer an alternative perspective on previous works focusing on terminal spanning ratio in facility location problems.

The Brück conjecture encompasses a broad framework of statements spanning several distinct areas of complex analysis, with a corresponding general formulation proposed by Brück in 1991. We have previously established a distinctive case of the Brück conjecture, focusing on entire solutions with hyperorders less than half. This paper delves into the reverse scenario, investigating solutions within specific classes where the hyperorder falls below a certain threshold. We derive new precise estimates concerning the relationship between the hyperorder and the difference order of meromorphic solutions, while also obtaining refined insights into the difference order of entire solutions relative to their hyperorders.

This research explores enhancing polynomial linear system solving through the use of closures, a technique that incorporates closures of Gröbner bases. We demonstrate how utilizing closures reduces the number of evaluations needed for arbitrary-precision arithmetic while solving polynomial linear systems, efficiently addressing systems with errors. Additionally, we broaden the application of closures to systems involving rational coefficients, thereby further expanding the scope of this method.

We describe a technique for producing controlled, multiphoton emissions, 
regardless of their parity, using a cavity QED system. By activating a rapid 
collapse reaction on a two-level atom via a coherent drive, we show that the 
emitted photons from the cavity can be set to have an even or odd number, 
noted as $\hat{d}_{+}(t)$ and $\hat{d}_{-}(t)$ respectively. When these 
emissions interact with a broad continuum environment, they evolve into Poisson 
distributed photon states, characterized by $\hat{a}_{+}(t)$ and $\hat{a}_{-}(t)$ 
respectively. We demonstrate that the even and odd photon states can be 
isolated through a technique involving frequency shifting, thereby enabling 
the production of controlled, multiphoton entanglement. We further show that 
$\langle \hat{a}^2 \rangle$ can be manipulated to follow a generalized Poisson 
distribution, with applications in the generation of secure, two-beam 
randomness for quantum randomness extraction. We also explore an application 
of this method in the production of quadrature entanglement via the squeezing 
of field modes in a cavity QED system.

We develop a unified equation of state for Group IA elements, which is designed to adhere to the principle of corresponding states. By combining experimental data from alkali molecules and theoretical calculations of their zero-zero pressure, we create an equation of state applicable across all alkali elements. This general equation of state enables the prediction of properties not only within isoelectronic sequences but also at pressures far exceeding those achievable experimentally.

The Chern-Simons term in vector-like gauge theories can be reconstructed through a gauge invariant derivative replacement in a specific way. This replacement maintains locality in the gauge field and is consistent across all orders. It's applied to the Dirac action of a quark in a perturbative, locally parity breaking medium, affecting the gluon and giving quarks kinetic and dynamical mass contributions. Furthermore, this replacement enables the incorporation of CS term effects in vector mesons, leading to a description similar to Dimopoulos-Milton's, with a modified kinematic mass term resulting. Our finding has potential implications for vector meson production in photon-proton collisions.

We introduce a randomized distributed algorithm designed to estimate the size of unknown networks. The approach relies on a single message exchange and does not require knowledge of network parameters beyond relying on nodes having the same probability distribution over their local neighbors. The accuracy of our method is assured under the condition that the symmetric degree distribution of the network does not vary significantly across its nodes. The mean absolute error and standard deviation of this estimate are analyzed, with theoretical results verified by both synthetic and real-world experiments.

Solving the Hamiltonian constraint in loop quantum gravity is a pressing issue. We address this challenge by developing a novel approach that transforms the Hamiltonian constraint into a transport equation. This transport equation can be solved using methods similar to those applied in cosmological models. Our method differs significantly from previous solutions that involved correcting conformal factors. We also propose a new technique for solving the Hamiltonian and dichotomy constraints within the loop quantum gravity framework. This approach reduces the two constraints to a transport equation and an elliptic equation, making its implementation more feasible.

The 20-kt underground neutrino experiment, JUNO, is based on a 19500-ton liquid-scintillator tank equipped with 19500 20kQ photomultiplier tubes sensitive to 20nm wavelengths, allowing it to detect low-energy neutrinos across an enormous energy range from 1eV to 100MeV. By harnessing the dual purposes of detecting solar neutrinos and accelerator neutrinos, as well as naturally occurring neutrinos from the Earth's interior, this research will investigate various neutrino phenomena, utilizing an event reconstruction program that is part of the JUNO software framework and supported by a dedicated team. This paper outlines the event reconstruction techniques specifically designed for detector calibration, neutrino research, and analysis within the JUNO experiment.

The Informer model excels at capturing long-term dependencies in time series, but its geographical version struggles with dimensionality challenges, where each dimension represents a different geographic location. This leads to the model treating each dimension separately and neglecting their interdependencies. To address this, we propose an enhanced geographical Informer model that combines dimension embeddings to facilitate the model in learning the interdimensional relationships. Experimental results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms the conventional Informer in multidimensional time series prediction, surpassing several prominent baselines by at least 4%.

Our analysis of various atmospheric dispersion correctors reveals that a crossed astigmatism corrector provides the best performance across multiple telescope types and spectral ranges. Further research aims to refine the cross astigmatism corrector to enhance its performance. The study centered on a 8.2-meter telescope at a specific location, striving to achieve minimal residual color across the entire visible spectrum. The results indicate that the refined cross astigmatism corrector yields residual colors an order of magnitude better than the original model, making it an excellent option for future ADC designs.

This paper introduces PILE, a novel ensemble method that utilizes label information to train, unlike traditional ensemble techniques. PILE's key component is a pairwise deep learning model that generates label-sensitive logits during training, and these are then aggregated from multiple models to form an iterative estimation of the data distribution according to the negative logarithm of its support. Our experiments show that PILE surpasses leading deep learning methods on several benchmarks, and its performance complements ensemble methods that focus on predicting class probabilities. Additionally, PILE's estimated distribution is utilized to improve traditional methods of class activation mapping and adversarial testing.

The current detection methods for bosonic dark matter are incapable of confirming the existing LDM model's predictions. Therefore, a new approach is needed to observe the small and widespread nature of LDM's signal. Using an array of sensors, we can improve our chances of detecting the random and periodic changes in the gravitational field produced by LDM. By taking into consideration the inherent noise present in each sensor, we have calculated the optimal sensor layout for an array of sensors. Our analysis shows that an array of sensors can significantly increase the area in which the LDM signal can be detected when compared to a single sensor experiment. Additionally, an array of sensors allows for the detection of smaller periodic signals, which can be missed by a single sensor experiment.

The basis pursuit problem, a sparse model-fitting task, relies heavily on the chosen representation matrix, whose spectral properties, particularly its extension to the 2nd power, play a crucial role in ensuring that sparse solutions are accurately represented. However, the underlying spectral problem is often intractable due to the size and complexity of the matrix. This study decomposes the matrix into two spectral components, allowing for the identification of necessary and sufficient conditions on these sums and products of singular values and values of vector norms for correctly capturing sparse solutions. These conditions are verified for several classes of random matrices, and a speculative conjecture on the performance of basis pursuit in low-rank tau-regularized least-squares problems is also presented.

Advances in programmable switches have led to numerous research applications,  yet vendor-provided switchrunners often restrict in-depth hardware access.  This hinders certain research domains that require customized OS-level driverssuch as third-party network stack development and tainted data isolation.  To bridge this gap, we suggest an open-source compiler backend for the  Flent network benchmark suite, enabling compilation of the benchmark into bare  machine code that can run on hardware with limited OS support.  This  facilitates research in various areas, including in-depth hardware testing,  development of third-party network stacks, and data isolation across different  systems.  To validate our work, we tested the open-source compiler on a Firebox  6.0.12 and observed results comparable to those run on a Linux-backed Firebox.  This  new backend allows us to investigate the creation of custom OS-level drivers  using low-level C code.  In a related domain, our work also enables the study  of data isolation across different systems through binary rewriting and  segmentation.  Furthermore, our network system architects can design and  analyze zero-day attacks in network switches, reinforcing the need for in-depth  hardware testing.

This study introduces a novel finite element approach that simultaneously solves a vector transport equation and a flow equation. The proposed method utilizes a mixed finite element discretization that incorporates vector fields and scalar fields. The introduction of penalty terms in the bilinear form allows for the incorporation of Dirichlet boundary conditions in the numerical solution. The approach is implemented in a 2D setting and tested under different flow regimes, including steady and unsteady conditions. The resulting method converges towards a stable solution as the mesh size approaches zero, and boundary conditions are accurately replicated. In particular, when a transport equation is driven by a laminar flow, the method yields solutions comparable to exact solutions. Furthermore, in cases involving chaotic regimes, the time-evolution of the transport field converges towards an asymptotic state as time progresses. The method's performance is also evaluated in terms of its sensitivity to different parameters and mesh types.

To address growing concerns about the ethical implications of machine learning, researchers are developing frameworks that combine fairness metrics, advanced techniques such as federated learning and differential privacy, and new metrics like fairness-deep learning. Despite the lack of standardization, these innovations show promising potential to enhance transparency and accountability in highly sensitive domains like healthcare.

A comprehensive LHCb experiment investigation has been conducted to search for the $B_c^+$ being produced in association with an excited $\Xi_c^0$ particle, specifically focusing on the decay mode $\Xi_c^0 	rightarrow \pi^- K^- J/\psi$. The data, gathered from proton-proton collisions with center-of-mass energy 13 TeV, totals 5.4 inverse femtobarns of luminosity. Through advanced analysis of the two-body decay spectrum of $B_c^+ 	rightarrow J/\psi \pi^+$, two previously unknown excited states of $B_c^+$ were identified at 6406.1 MeV and 6410.2 MeV, with their properties being described by quark-level dynamics. Furthermore, the observed occurrences of these two $B_c^+$ excited states were found to match the expected predictions for their production. The analysis also yields a measurement for the branching fraction of the $\Xi_c^0$ decaying into $\pi^- K^- J/\psi$ at $1.0 \pm 0.3 \pm 0.3 \pm 0.2$ percent, with the stated margins for uncertainty respectively.

Our investigation begins by exploring the theoretical foundations of continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods. We delve into their connection to discrete-stage Runge-Kutta methods, and establish how certain continuous-stage methods can be seen as generating sequences of Lagrangian flows for Hamiltonian problems. We also identify certain constraints on their generating vectors that ensure exact preservation of the Poisson structure. Under certain conditions, we develop new constraints on these vectors that guarantee nearby solutions remain approximately close. We develop explicit conditions under which continuous-stage methods can be seen as generating flows for Hamiltonian systems. The theoretical framework we develop is based on analyzing the flow of certain differential equations that describe the flow of a phase space's boundary. We develop new numerical methods for solving Hamiltonian problems and reducing secular errors in polar methods, and show that certain continuous-stage methods can be seen as generating solutions to these problems. We develop a new criterion for determining whether a point is "close enough" to a phase space's boundary, and use this to create new numerical methods for reducing secular errors in polar methods. Our investigation also connects the analysis of continuous-stage methods to previously-studied problems in mathematical physics.

Model updates in distributed neural network training often incur significant computation and communication costs. In this paper, we address these challenges by introducing an efficient local critic training method that speeds up the training process of convolutional and recurrent neural networks. By leveraging our previous finding that efficient updates stem from approximating the gradient direction, we propose three novel all-at-once algorithms framework and show that an existing method belongs to this category. We also demonstrate that local critic training is applicable across various network architectures, resulting in substantial performance gains for parameter-tight RNNs. Notably, our training method achieves a communication complexity of O(Rr^2) for convolutional networks and O(r^2) for recurrent networks, where r represents the number of recurrent units, significantly reducing communication overhead compared to the O(r^3) complexity of traditional batch gradient descent.

In a region of chaotic scattering known as a Wada basin, multiple sink domains meet at a single point, forming a tripartite boundary. Typically, this unique structure causes scattered trajectories to converge to one of the sinks regardless of their initial location. Introducing low-level dissipation, however, is found to destabilize this stable behavior, ultimately leading to changes in the boundary's shape and the formation of a wedge-like area where trajectories are susceptible to being drawn to any of the three sinks. Increasing dissipation leads to further significant transformations of the boundary, resulting in a shape akin to a balanced scale, solely based on the ratio of dissipation rates for two separate systems.

To resolve the muon g-2 anomaly, we need an experiment with exceptional sensitivity, 
reaching a precision at least 1E-17 in the new Wilson coefficient $d_\mu$, 
within the context of the electroweak gauge boson loop contribution model. 
A proposed future experiment, LePnFV, aimed at investigating the $d_\mu$ space, 
is now envisioned to serve this purpose, 
as it will employ a high-intensity muon beam from a muon collider or ultrarelativistic 
proton or heavy-ion beams from an $e$+$e$+$\mu$ collider. 
We have recalled the parameters of the experiment, 
notably its capacity for an angular acceptance of 20 to 50 mrad, 
reaching a count rate of 1 to 10 events per muon transition per second, 
with an event selection efficiency of 10 to 40 percent. 
Due to its relatively conservative parameters, 
LePnFV can still maintain a highly versatile physics program, 
accommodating a wide range of beam conditions and physics targets, 
as it is designed to globally optimize its sensitivity to anomalous muon g-2. 
In this study, 
we investigate the adjustable parameters of LePnFV, 
its potential for analyzing various physics phenomena, 
including single-photon and transverse muon decay, 
as well as the decay of a transverse

This paper introduces Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN), an innovative model that utilizes hierarchical temporal attention mechanisms to prioritize multiple aspects within sequential data. By merging temporal and spatial attention at the frame level, HAN emphasizes crucial objects corresponding to previously prioritized regions in time. Additionally, the multi-step spatial temporal attention mechanism enables reasoning beyond a single step, allowing the model to consider relationships between objects. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HAN in resolving the body pose estimation problem from video data.

Using the quantum field-theory framework of $2d$ CFTs, we've investigated the interaction between a black hole and a scalar field in the far future of the black hole's event horizon. Our study, conducted using the Hamiltonian and Bogoliubov transformations, reveals that near-extremal and extremal black holes retain memory of the interaction, in contrast to intermediate mass black holes. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that our findings align with the predictions of quantum mechanics and effective field theories, while also providing a future-based validation of the holographic theorem.

The exploration of star formation across diverse galaxies allows us to examine the fundamental process by which the raw materials of the universe give rise to life, lighting up the cosmos in the process. By dissecting galaxies of every description, spanning from massive ellipticals to sprawling spirals and distant, actively bursting galaxies, researchers have gained profound insights into the complex evolution of the universe. Star formation is not only driving galactic evolution but also shaping the environment through the expulsion of supermassive black holes and influencing the composition of the interstellar medium. As result, the study of star formation is integral to an in-depth understanding of galaxy development and the intricate web of the universe. A comprehensive review of the subject is presented here, covering recent breakthroughs in star formation research through the examination of local galaxies.

In various scenarios, it's essential to calculate entropies from observed data, but some distributions aren't known directly, making it difficult to compute their entropies numerically. 

I propose a novel method to estimate the entropy of a target distribution, even when the underlying probability distribution is inaccessible. 

My approach relies on analyzing the known marginal distributions of the target distribution. 

Since entropy is a fixed linear transformation of probability distributions, the marginal distributions are projected onto a lower-dimensional space, and then I minimize the difference between the original marginal entropies and those produced by optimizing the distribution over the projected space, using a gradient descent method. 

This process is repeated iteratively until convergence, allowing for the estimation of the entropy of the original distribution. 

The method works theoretically for any observable $X$ and has been successfully tested in simulations and real-world cases.

In the context of semiconductor production, highly complex and dynamically interconnected systems rely on sophisticated control mechanisms to optimize their performance. The interdependence of these systems' components and their interaction with continuous physical processes render mathematical modeling and traditional control strategies challenging to apply. A novel modeling approach utilizes measure-theoretic ideas to frame states and fluxes as Borel measures, facilitating the efficient modeling of these complex systems. This measure-theoretic framework enables precise modeling of the dynamics and evolution of semiconductor systems, including processes like etching, chemical vapor deposition, and photolithography. The associated literature is relatively sparse, offering few relevant findings to guide state observation and control efforts. Recent research results are presented in a concise manner.

Classifying network attacks is becoming increasingly essential to enhance device security, but developing reliable models to run efficiently on resource-constrained devices remains a challenge. High-quality models often exceed device capabilities, causing them to fail in deployment. To overcome this issue, we have developed NBcoded, an innovative tool combining Bayesian coding and transfer learning to create compact, accurate, and interpretable models that can seamlessly run on devices. NBcoded leverages the statistical relationships between network traffic features and attack labels encoded in probability distributions to predict attacks, utilizing a specialized, efficient coding technique that minimizes data size without sacrificing readability. Through thorough evaluation, NBcoded demonstrates superior performance on limited-resource devices, surpassing conventional models by substantial margins. For example, NBcoded achieves a remarkable 14.23% error reduction on Raspberry Pi 3 devices and 8.41% on Intel NUC devices.

The residual width of metabelian groups from higher up in their lower central series has been largely unexplored. The number of groups that a metabelian group can have within its class family is infinite, yet this study shows that such groups have a limited range of growth rates. The research finds that for any metabelian group, the ratio of its nilpotent rank to the growth rate is capped at 1/2. The study also establishes that for infinite metabelian groups with no torsion, the growth rate is at most twice their nilpotent rank. Furthermore, this research shows that for finitely presented metabelian groups, the growth rate is at most twice their nilpotent rank. The study provides examples to confirm these upper limits are, in some cases, precisely achieved.

In our daily lives, videos show us the movements of various objects, providing essential information about what's happening around us. Identifying living things in video sequences can reveal their behaviors, which are often full of meaning. Distinguishing the movements of living things from the movements of non-biological objects is possible by analyzing the ways in which their parts move and the shapes they take. The way the parts of the human body move and their shapes provide clues about what's happening inside the body, like the movement of the heart or the movement of the eyes focusing on something. Similarly, the shapes and movements of agricultural products can reveal information about their health, and the patterns of plant growth can indicate seasonal changes. The movement patterns of vehicles can also be used to track the movement of drivers' hands and heads. So, recognizing the movements of living things and their parts in video sequences can provide valuable insights that can be used in many areas, like studying the human body, monitoring agricultural crops, and following vehicle movements. We've developed an approach called LMS, which uses features that don't change as much as possible to identify the movements of these objects and their parts accurately and robustly. By looking at the ways in which objects and their parts move and the shapes they take, we've discovered features that help us tell the movements of living things apart from the movements of non-biological objects, and the movements of their different parts apart from the movements of the same objects' undivided shapes.
